articles.title: What if we paid for electricity through taxes, not bills?
articles.author: Colin Nolden, Senior Research Fellow, Energy Institute, University of Sheffield
paras: The UK government has announced that standing charges will be removed from gas bills and that it intends to also remove them from electricity bills. Standing charges are a fixed fee paid by every household, regardless of how much they use. Under the proposed change, the costs they cover would instead be covered through unit rates, thereby ensuring that the costs are spread more fairly among those using more or less gas.

The budget also extends a temporary suspension of VAT on electricity and introduces a one-off payment of £100 to households in council tax bands A-D. Together, these measures might shave around £130 off the average annual energy bill for struggling households.

In principle, this announcement is welcome. But with energy bills expected to increase by £400 annually from January, these measures raise a bigger question: how should Britain pay for the energy system transformation away from fossil fuels? What if more of the costs were covered through taxation rather than bills?

Energy bills don’t just reflect the cost of supplying electricity and gas. They also include “policy costs”, which fund the greening of the energy system (around 60%) and support for vulnerable households (40%).
These costs add around £300 a year to the average household bill, accounting for around 16% of a typical electricity bill and 6% of a typical gas bill, according to research by Nesta.

Recovering these costs through electricity bills is a political choice that made more sense when electricity generation was mainly coal-fired and highly polluting. Now that the share of renewables is increasing steadily, we should reconsider how these policy costs are paid. Policy costs have roughly doubled in the past decade, making electricity relatively more expensive than gas, which slows the shift to electrified heating and transport.
The government has already taken steps towards shifting costs from bills to taxation.

In its 2025 autumn statement, the government moved 75% of the costs of the Renewables Obligation – an old policy support mechanism for renewable energy – into general taxation. It also disbanded a flagship but discredited home insulation scheme entirely. This was expected to lower bills by around £150 per year, before geopolitical turmoil pushed prices up again.

The latest budget provides a further example of this approach. Alongside the announcement to remove standing charges from bills, ministers have scrapped a planned levy on gas bills to fund hydrogen projects, deciding instead to pay for them through government funding.
The UK’s official advisory Climate Change Committee has also recommended removing policy levies from electricity bills to make electricity cheaper and accelerate electrification.

Energy UK, the industry’s main trade body, has gone further, arguing for shifting policy costs off electricity and onto a mix of taxation and gas bills. This would make gas relatively more expensive, encouraging electrification and renewable energy.
Other groups, including parts of the chemical industry, warn that raising gas prices could make the industry less competitive by significantly raising industrial costs.
In principle, shifting costs from bills to taxation moves money between largely the same people. However, the distributional effects are different.
Instead of a flat fee on everyone’s bill, a tax-funded system would be “progressive”. This means the more you earn, the more you contribute.

By contrast, the current system of levies – with a fixed charge added to everyone’s energy bill – is “regressive”. Because those charges are the same for everyone, they take a much larger chunk out of a low-income household’s budget than a wealthy one’s.

This means poorer households not only spend a greater share of their income on energy, but many of the green subsidies funded by the levies – such as support for electric vehicles or heat pumps – disproportionately benefit wealthier households.

But why stop there? Analysts at the New Economics Foundation, a thinktank, argue for funding a basic level of energy use through taxation. The taxpayer would keep your lights on and your fridge running, but you’d think twice before charging your electric vehicle in the more expensive peak hours.

Thinktank E3G’s work suggests this could cut household bills by around £300 a year, at a cost of £10-11 billion per year to 2030. Some of this could potentially be covered by higher tax revenues from oil and gas companies during periods of high prices, the thinktank argues.
It would be an intervention on a similar scale to the £40 billion the UK government spent on subsiding bills during the 2022-23 energy crisis sparked by Russia’s invasion of the Ukraine.

Another option is a rising block tariff, in which energy use is divided into tiers, or “blocks”, and households pay progressively more as their usage increases. Its proponents suggest block tariffs can make energy more affordable while aligning with wider decarbonisation goals.

In practice, however, these tariffs are likely to be regressive, since people on lower incomes are more likely to live in poorly-insulated homes and rely on less efficient electric night storage heating.

The government can do little to influence the effect of geopolitical uncertainty on energy prices, and drilling in the North Sea will do nothing to lower household bills. What it can do is change how those prices are passed on to consumers.

Shifting policy costs to taxation is already under way. But maybe the time is right for a minimum or essential energy use supported through taxation. It is not a simple solution, and many trade-offs need to be considered, but an unprecedented shock to energy markets requires an unprecedented response.

Colin Nolden researches sustainable energy and climate governance at the intersection of markets, policy, places, and people. He is currently funded by the Energy Demand Research Centre (EDRC). Colin also works as a specialist advisor of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, as an expert peer-reviewer for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and as a non-executive director of Community Energy Pathways.

articles.title: England needs 120% of normal rainfall to come out of drought this winter – storms won’t fix that yet
articles.author: Hannah Cloke, Regius Professor of Meteorology and Climate Science, University of Reading
paras: Storm Austen and Storm Boelo swept across the UK in quick succession. Rain lashed windows, river levels rose and the clocks went back. It feels like winter has arrived all at once.

Yet most of England and Wales are still in drought. Parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset and Sussex are in severe drought, the highest level the Environment Agency can declare. South-west and south-east England have had their driest April to September in over 100 years.

But how can this be when it is cold, dark and pouring with rain? Drought tightens or loosens its grip over months, not just a few days. It will be the rainy or dry nature of the months ahead that will decide whether the drought ends, or more worryingly, if it stays into next summer.
Winter should fill the tank

Summer droughts grab the headlines and public attention. When we have a dry period over the summer it’s everywhere, with brown lawns, hosepipe bans and cracked reservoir beds. But winter is when the UK refills its water stores.

Between October and March, with shorter and colder days, less water evaporates and plants drink far less, so rain finally has the chance to refill our reservoirs. Rain can soak deep into the ground to top up groundwater, the water held in chalk and sandstone rocks beneath our feet, like a giant sponge. Groundwater supplies much of the drinking water in southern and eastern England, but it fills slowly, over months and years.

Think of it like a bank account. A hot summer is a big splurge with lots of withdrawals. But a dry winter means the deposits needed to repay that spending never arrive. That’s why a dry winter can do more damage to our water supplies than a heatwave.

This year the account is badly overdrawn. Southern England has just had its driest April to September in more than a century, alongside record summer heat. The Wimbleball reservoir on Exmoor, which supplies around 400,000 people, was full in March, after an extremely wet winter. Then the weather shifted from wetter than normal to dryer than normal. By October, water levels at Wimbleball were down to about 13%.
How unusual is a winter drought?

Droughts that carry on into winter are rare in the UK. Usually the autumn rain arrives, soil gets wetter and water stores recover by Christmas. Every instinct suggests that a stormy autumn should fix things.

In the 2010 to 2012 drought, two dry winters in a row left groundwater in south and east England so low that hosepipe bans came in during spring 2012. Then the wettest April on record arrived, and parts of the country swung from drought to flood within weeks.
What stands out now is how quickly droughts are stacking up. This is the third drought in England in five years. The stores barely have time to recover before the next one begins.

England and Wales can be in drought and experience flooding simultaneously. After months of dry weather it takes a lot of rain to wet the ground all the way through. Storms such as Boelo and Austen bring bursts of heavy rain. Drains are overwhelmed and rivers rise quickly, sometimes spilling out onto their floodplains. But the reservoirs and groundwater that supply our taps respond far more slowly, and need lots of water to fill up. So the type of winter rains make a big difference.

Floods can hit fast. But the key parts of the water cycle are slow. Rain has to wet the soil all the way through before it can trickle down into the rock, and groundwater can take months to respond. The Environment Agency estimates England needs around 120% of normal rainfall between September and April for every area to come out of drought. We would need half a year with consistently more rain than we would expect at this time of year to break this drought.
If rain falls short across the whole winter, then England could start next summer in drought, with even less room for manoeuvre.
Will winter droughts become more common?

But climate scientists don’t expect there will be a dry winter every year, either now or in decades ahead as fossil fuel burning continues to heat the planet. Climate projections suggest UK winters will get wetter on average. But averages can hide the danger.

Summers heated by the burning of fossil fuels dry out the soil and drain reservoirs faster, leaving a bigger hole for winter to fill. Winter rain is increasingly arriving in heavy bursts that are harder to capture and more likely to flood. And natural swings in the weather will still deliver dry winters from time to time. Put those together and the chance of a drought rolling into winter, or across two winters, goes up. This is a trend that will keep getting worse as long as we keep heating the planet.
Preparing starts with how we think about water. It is precious, not endless. Yet we have built a system that lets a wet winter rush away to the sea, then rations what is left through a dry summer.

As with other parts of the UK’s water system, we are paying the price now for years of chronic underinvestment. Water companies need to move much faster on fixing leaks, which still waste billions of litres every day. New reservoirs are being planned in England, which will help deliver more storage. But they will take more than a decade to build, cost billions of pounds, and cannot be the whole solution.

There is also a low-tech local answer, that would need regulation and a programme of retrofitting to make a big difference. Rainwater harvesting and water reuse in new and existing homes, sustainable drainage in our towns, and encouraging wetlands and floodplains that hold water like a sponge.
Changes to our landscape and homes can help prevent both problems.
Each of us can help. Take shorter showers, ask your water company about a meter and and fit a water butt to catch rain for the garden. These habits add up.
Autumn storms have started to replenish water reserves, but it’s not the finish line. We also need to get ahead of what is likely to happen in years to come.

Hannah Cloke advises the Environment Agency, the European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasts, the Copernicus Emergency Management Service, local and national governments and humanitarian agencies on the forecasting and warning of natural hazards. She is a fellow of the European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasts. Her research is funded by the UKRI Engineering & Physical Sciences Research Council, the UKRI Natural Environment Research Council, the European Commission and the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office.

articles.title: Werewolf mice, ghostly frogs and zombie cockroaches: the animal versions of our Halloween horrors
articles.author: Alex Dittrich, Senior Lecturer in Zoology, Nottingham Trent University
paras: Around this time of year, elaborate decorations featuring ghosts, vampires, zombies, witches and werewolves adorn front doors, gardens and shop windows across the country.
But you may be surprised to hear that in the animal world, there are many real-life creatures with similar tendencies to these fictional characters of our Halloween nightmares.

The southern grasshopper mouse (Onychomys torridus) howls at the moon to defend its territory and attract mates, a little like werewolves in films. These nocturnal rodents stand up on their hind legs, point their nose upwards, and produce high-pitched sounds.

Grasshopper mice are voracious carnivores, preying upon scorpions, beetles, grasshoppers, and even other mice. They are also immune to the stings of their favourite food – the bark scorpion (Centruroides sculpturatus). Grasshopper mice can block the chemical pathway that transmits the signal from the venom, essentially numbing themselves to the pain. They then bite off the scorpion’s tail, rendering their prey defenseless to their fate.
These little rodents are so formidable that they will unhesitatingly attack anything that is appropriately sized and considered to be food, even if it might be dangerous.

Small mammals, like grasshopper mice, play crucial ecological roles in their ecosystems. For example, through digging their burrows, they can act as ecosystem engineers (species that modify the environment) creating microhabitats for other species.

The emerald jewel wasp (Ampulex compressa) is a stunningly beautiful and ecologically important species. Not only do they act as casual pollinators for a range of plant species, they are also an essential biocontrol; an organism that controls the population of a pest species.

Over millions of years they have evolved the morbid ability to sting cockroaches and turn them into compliant zombies upon which they lay their eggs. When these eggs hatch, the larvae devour the zombified cockroach from the inside out.

Small birds called oxpeckers (Buphagus species) and large ungulates (hoofed mammals) were considered to have a mutually beneficial relationship. When these birds removed pesky ticks and other parasites from their mammalian companions, they were rewarded with a quick, tasty meal. Oxpeckers are often spotted travelling around on the backs of these larger animals.

However, research has highlighted that this relationship may be more complicated than previously thought. Oxpeckers will pick at open wounds to consume blood and flesh – inflicting injuries, preventing wound-healing, and increasing the risk of infection in their hosts.

Witches are well known for creating magical potions but some insects do this too. Bombardier beetles can blast would-be predators with explosive chemicals discharged from their abdomens at temperatures of 100°C. They do this by mixing hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide within their bodies in a small reaction chamber – their cauldron, if you will – to create this explosion.

Some other insects use chemicals not as a defence mechanism, but to woo a mate. This isn’t an elixir of love, but instead the combination of a chemical and an enzyme (Luciferin and luciferase) that causes a beautiful, if slightly eerie, glow.

The fireflies of the family Lampyridae are actually beetles, whose males flash these colours enthusiastically to attract a waiting female from the undergrowth. Beauty and intrigue aside, fireflies are useful throughout their native range. As larvae they feed on many soft-bodied invertebrates, preventing pest outbreaks and maintaining maintaining a natural equilibrium of species in the soil and leaf litter.
Some frogs in the family Centrolenidae are so translucent, or ghost-like, that they have become known as glass frogs.

Found in the tropical forests of Central and South America, these extraordinary frogs spend much of their lives in the trees and play an important role in the ecosystem. They help regulate insect populations through predation and act as prey for a variety of other species, including in aquatic food webs as tadpoles inhabiting streams. In many ways, they occupy multiple levels of the rainforest ecosystem, linking both terrestrial and freshwater environments.

Come Halloween, many people embellish their houses with plastic skeletons and toilet-paper clad mummies. One insect does a similar thing – the aptly named bone-house wasp (Deuteragenia ossarium). Known for hunting another Halloween favourite, the spider, it decorates the nests it makes for its young with a pile of ant corpses. This morbid tableau provides sensory camouflage for the nest, keeping intruders well away.

All these species are important components of their ecosystems – from keeping pest populations in check or being prey themselves for other animals, to acting as ecological indicators allowing us to monitor environmental changes. Ecological indicator species are key species within ecosystems that help us understand more about how our impact on the planet is affecting other species. Animals respond to different things in the environment, so their populations and behaviours can indicate whether the environment is changing for the better or worse.

These animals may have some rather terrifying tendencies, but unlike the fantasy characters of our horror-film nightmares, they don’t disappear after All Hallows’ Eve. They also have real environmental benefits that endure.

articles.title: Drones could help weather forecasters more accurately predict winter storms
articles.author: Declan Finney, Senior Research Fellow in Cloud Physics, University of Leeds
paras: Weather drones are being tested to help update forecasts of extreme weather more quickly, and could help us prepare earlier for upcoming winter storms.

With an unprecedented El Niño increasing the chance of storms and wet weather in Europe this winter, meteorologists will be looking at new and developing tools to help them forecast as accurately as possible.
The ability of new types of weather drones to collect more information ahead of incoming bad weather has already attracted the attention of financial traders.

Energy traders have to buy and sell electricity produced from sources like wind and solar farms. They need to judge the supply and demand as quickly as possible. This means they need updates to weather forecasts so they can predict when clouds might shade solar panels, or if an approaching storm could increase wind turbine generation.

US researchers have recently highlighted that the ability of drones to collect information on air pressure and wind speed, for instance, in real time is proving useful for forecasting extreme weather events faster.

Meanwhile, UK researchers are pushing the technology further by using drones to collect valuable data inside clouds. Clouds are fundamental to many weather effects, including rain, fog, lightning, hail and extreme winds.

In 2024, the World Meteorological Organisation hosted its first demonstration of weather drones. These drones measured temperature and wind speed, and focused on the lowest few kilometres of the atmosphere.

This use of drones is being developed with the expectation that they can be used as part of a network of drone stations by meteorological agencies, to complement traditional networks of weather stations.

These drones can be deployed remotely from a dock, allowing routine measurement of the lower atmosphere to inform weather forecasts. This is similar to how weather balloons currently operate. Drones, however, have the potential to provide data at much higher frequency, and more quickly. Data could be collected hourly or more often, and with less waste such as lost weather balloon equipment.

A new research project, Drone Observation Of Clouds (DOOC), led by the University of Leeds, is working out if new kinds of measurement could become part of weather forecasting in the future. They are looking at measuring the most uncertain component of weather and climate, clouds.

Between June and November 2026 DOOC has been flying and collecting measurements at a site in Yorkshire, UK. Leeds-based drone operator, Menapia, has collaborated with University of Leeds to obtain permission to fly in an unusually narrow column of air up to 1,600 metres.

That small section of airspace enables a weather drone to measure temperature, humidity, wind and cloud particles at all heights between the ground and 1,600 metres. At only 30m wide, this narrow piece of airspace only makes sense for a rotor drone that can ascend perfectly vertically.

A particle counter is mounted on the drone and can determine the size and concentration of cloud droplets. It has been developed and tested for almost a decade, honing it to be suitable for drone-based measurement.
The DOOC project will build on recent forecasting advances at the UK Met Office. UK forecasts now use a much more detailed representation of cloud physics to make forecasts more accurate.

Drone-based measurements of weather and clouds could offer the next breakthroughs in the rapidly growing field of AI weather forecasting. AI weather forecasting leans more heavily on data than traditional forecasting methods. So, the collection of routine observations of the atmosphere has become more important than ever.

As US researchers are also finding, one of the greatest challenges is how to work with regulators to enable drone operation for research alongside traditional air users, as well as commercial and military drone users.
Scientists are arguing for new infrastructure investment and regulatory support to make the most of this developing drone technology.

Drone observations have the potential to greatly benefit wider society through the improved weather forecasts, which will mean the ability to prepare better for upcoming extreme weather earlier, and potentially put protection in place.

articles.title: Key Atlantic currents could collapse this century, but the risk is missing from almost all national climate plans – new study
articles.author: Brenden Jongman, Honorary Research Associate, Environmental Change Institute, University of Oxford
paras: Icelandic government officials recently met to discuss a dramatic scenario: what if the current that circulates Atlantic waters weakened significantly, or collapsed altogether?

The ocean currents are changing, with major implications for climate around the world. Yet our new research suggests most governments are not preparing for this possibility. Of 91 national adaptation plans submitted to the UN climate convention, only two even mention that key Atlantic current, and neither sets out concrete action in response to its possible collapse.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or Amoc, is part of the giant conveyor belt of ocean currents that moves warm surface water northward in the Atlantic and sends colder deep water back south. It plays a critical role in regulating the global climate by redistributing heat around the planet, influencing weather patterns and temperatures far beyond the Atlantic basin.

As the climate warms, the Amoc is weakening, and could continue to do so throughout this century. While a full collapse, in which major ocean currents completely reorientate, is unlikely before 2100, a recent study projected a 50% weakening of the Amoc by the end of the century under an intermediate emissions scenario. A collapse would not be unique in geological history. Studies show that the Amoc has undergone dramatic changes before, including a near-complete shutdown around 17,500 years ago, after the coldest period in the last ice age.

A slowdown or collapse would have major implications for temperature and rainfall around the world. In northern Europe, the loss of the heat Amoc transfers northwards from the tropics could lead to winter cold extremes of -20°C in London.

Climate model experiments in which the Amoc is shut down show an average 29% weakening of the West African monsoons and 19% weakening of the Indian summer monsoon, increasing risks of food and water insecurity in regions that rely on monsoon rains. Other studies suggest an increased risk of severe drought in parts of Central America, West Africa and the Amazon region. Fisheries and sea level would also be affected.

So how can countries prepare for changes in ocean circulation whose timing is highly uncertain? Our research identifies practical steps to incorporate Amoc-related risks into adaptation decision-making.
Most investments assume only gradual change

Of the 91 national adaptation plans reported to the UN climate convention so far, only two mention the Amoc. Brazil’s plan devotes a dedicated box to warning that its shutdown could push the Atlantic rain belt southwards, tipping the Amazon rainforest towards collapse. Ireland – which relies on the Amoc to sustain its mild climate – mentions that “reliance solely on adaptation may prove insufficient” in case of Amoc collapse, concluding that no national plan can prepare for such tipping points.

Amoc is a particular challenge for adaptation. It represents a very high impact scenario whose likelihood is very difficult to quantify. And yet if the current were to collapse, some parts of the world could experience climate changes in the opposite direction to those they are preparing for, most notably colder winters in north-western Europe.

This is important because many adaptation investments need to be robust to a wide range of potential changes to be effective. Consider a country planning to build a new reservoir to cope with more variable rainfall amounts under climate change. If instead the rainy season becomes shorter and there is less rain overall, the reservoir may seem like a bad investment.

Similarly, in countries that depend on monsoon rains, a weakening or collapse of the Amoc could mean even less rainfall than is projected under climate change. Along Atlantic coastlines, changes in sea level and ocean temperatures could affect how well coastal defences work. Changes in fish stocks could also threaten communities that depend on fishing.

Many investments made now will remain in use for decades. Investments that perform well under moderate Amoc weakening but poorly if the current weakened much more could expose countries to major losses and damages, especially poorer countries with fewer resources to respond to surprises.
Five ways to prepare for major Amoc weakening
In our study, we outline five ways policymakers can start preparing now.

1. Identify the investments and countries most at risk. Countries that rely heavily on monsoon rainfall, fisheries, or have major investments along the Atlantic coast may be especially exposed, as are countries with limited ability to respond to surprises.

2. Stress-test key investments. This means using computer simulations with Amoc-collapse scenarios to check whether these investments would still achieve their intended purpose under very different conditions, such as changes in temperature, sea level or rainfall.

3. Favour flexible solutions. Choose investments that can be adapted or expanded as conditions change, such as infrastructure projects that are built in stages or are easily upgradeable, or wide diversity of water supply or coastal defence options.

4. Use Amoc monitoring to inform adaptation decisions. Sustained funding for ocean monitoring is needed to track changes in ocean circulation, but governments should also regularly reassess whether their adaptation investments remain effective as our knowledge of Atlantic currents evolves.

5. Reassess global climate projections. Explore the implications of major Amoc weakening or collapse for global climate projections, including estimates of future warming. The Amoc influences how much carbon the oceans absorb from the atmosphere, so changes in its circulation could affect both how countries adapt to climate changes and how much further warming they need to prepare for.

These actions do not require predicting whether or when the Amoc will collapse, and should not take attention or resources away from responding to heatwaves, droughts, floods and other impacts of climate change that already happening. Efforts to rapidly cut greenhouse gas emissions remain crucial.

What countries can do is start testing long-term investments against scenarios involving major Amoc weakening, helping to ensure that infrastructure, water supplies and other adaptations remain effective in all plausible futures.

articles.title: Where humans build, mosquitoes follow – bringing dengue, West Nile and other diseases with them
articles.author: Kylee Rae Noel, Postdoctoral Research Associate in Entomology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
paras: A mosquito buzzing in your backyard may seem like a minor annoyance. But these tiny insects, with their taste for human blood, are increasingly appearing in areas where they were once rare or absent, and that’s raising concerns about the spread of mosquito-borne diseases, including West Nile, Zika and dengue fever.
Florida’s struggles with dengue fever in 2026 should be a warning.

Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, had seen more than 350 dengue cases, at least one of them fatal, by late October. Miami-Dade County had reported more than 200 cases, and the statewide number was still rising in what has been described as the largest dengue outbreak in modern Florida history. More than 400 of the over 700 Florida cases, including many of those in Hillsborough County and at least seven in the Orlando area, were listed as locally acquired from mosquitoes in the area.

Climate change is part of the reason people in many parts of the country are seeing more mosquitoes. Rising global temperatures and shorter winters expand the area suitable for mosquitoes to live in and transmit viruses that cause diseases. Climate change also brings increasingly erratic storm systems, heat and rainfall patterns that leave standing water, creating conditions ideal for mosquitoes to breed.
The other major factor shaping where mosquitoes live, often overlooked, is humans themselves.

We study entomology and medical geography, including the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. To understand why you may be seeing more mosquitoes, and why communities like Hillsborough County are spending millions of dollars on attempts to control them, start by looking close to home.
Mosquitoes follow when humans move in

Mosquitoes such as Aedes aegypti – the primary transmitter of pathogens that cause dengue fever, yellow fever, Chikungunya and Zika in the Americas – likely arrived in the U.S. with the slave trade. Both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, a transmitter of many of the same diseases but a more recent arrival in the U.S., are moved by the global shipping network, which can take them to new locations and reintroduce them in parts of their ranges where they may have been controlled in the past.
Aedes aegypti’s habits, including its ability to use household environments for living and breeding, have made it a very successful and established invader where climate conditions permit.

A flowerpot saucer, clogged gutter, discarded tire, birdbath or even a bottle cap can collect enough water for mosquito larvae to develop. A single Aedes aegypti mosquito can lay more than 100 eggs at a time up to five times during its lifespan, which is only about a month.
As suburban neighborhoods expand, so do opportunities for mosquitoes to breed and find humans for their meals.
Across the United States, new housing developments create thousands of these small water-holding containers and bring together the two things these mosquitoes need: standing water and people.

This combination allows them to spread through transportation networks, establishing populations far from their original ranges, and explains why mosquito expansion is often linked to patterns of human movement and development.

Aedes albopictus, originally native to Southeast Asia and now found in all habitable continents, provides a striking example of this spread. These mosquitoes arrived in the U.S. mostly because of human actions. They stowed away on boats and other vehicles, often riding in used tires or lucky bamboo.

Their early dispersal in the U.S. has been linked to the interstate highway system. By 2017, Aedes albopictus was documented in 1,368 counties across 40 states, and it has continued to expand across much of the eastern and central U.S.
One of Iowa’s first established Aedes albopictus populations, for example, appeared in the Des Moines metropolitan area, where it has continued to grow and expand to other communities.
Its spread from southeast Asia all the way to the U.S. Midwest demonstrates how globalization and suburban growth can create opportunities for mosquitoes.
US’s most common mosquito threat: West Nile

West Nile virus remains the most widespread mosquito-borne disease in the continental United States. It is primarily transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, including common house mosquitoes, which are found in much of the country.

Culex mosquitoes can breed in a wide range of habitats, including storm drains, roadside ditches, retention ponds, wetlands and other standing water. Their ability to thrive in both urban and rural environments has helped make West Nile virus an enduring public health concern in many states.

Because Culex mosquitoes are already established across much of the country, climate change may not necessarily introduce them to new regions. Instead, research is increasingly focused on how changing temperatures and precipitation patterns could influence their abundance, seasonal activity and ability to transmit disease.
Researchers found that New York state’s season with temperatures suitable for mosquitoes to transmit West Nile virus lengthened by an average of 20 days between 1999 and 2024.

A study conducted by one of us, Sadie Ryan, showed that in Florida, all 67 counties had a suitable season for mosquitoes spreading West Nile virus for five or more months in 2000, and 2.33 million people in Florida experienced a nine-month-long season. By the 2030s, as temperatures warm, the study projects that around 70% of Florida’s population is likely to have a chance of getting West Nile nine months out of the year.

In 2025, for example, Florida took longer to cool down in the fall than usual, leaving moderate temperatures and enough standing water that Aedes mosquitoes could remain active late into the year. Florida saw a rise in dengue cases.
Longer warm seasons means mosquitoes will become a growing public health issue, and controlling them will become increasingly crucial.

articles.title: Indonesia’s El Niño-driven peat fires are choking the region – and releasing centuries of stored carbon
articles.author: Gareth Roberts, Associate Professor, School of Geography and Environmental Science, University of Southampton
paras: Right now, people in parts of Indonesia are inhaling what may be the most polluted atmosphere on Earth. As the historically large 2026 El Niño intensifies, parts of south east Asia have been plunged into an air quality crisis of catastrophic proportions.
Smoke from fires has driven concentrations of dangerous and tiny particulate matter, known as PM2.5, to extreme levels – creating a public health emergency threatening millions of lives.

The World Health Organization (WHO) stipulates a maximum breathable “safe limit” of 15 micrograms per cubic metre of PM2.5 across a 24-hour average. In haze affected parts of Indonesia, this year’s concentrations have routinely exceeded 500 micrograms, and even 1,000 in places – that’s more than 65 times the WHO maximum.

This is not the kind of polluted air you might find on a smoggy day in most parts of the world – it is a toxic atmosphere considered by the US Environmental Protection Agency to be “hazardous”. The delayed effects of breathing such air include increased risk of heart attack, stroke and a host of respiratory illnesses.

The catalyst for this year’s crisis is a collision between meteorological events and decades of changes to Indonesia’s landscape. The historically intense El Niño has brought a punishing dry spell across the archipelago, leaving the landscape parched.
But the weather is only the match; land management practices provide the fuel.

Historically, lowland tropical forests growing on peat soils were naturally resistant to fire because of their moist conditions. However, deforestation for agriculture, forest fragmentation and peatland drainage have drastically altered the landscape and increased its flammability.

The effects can extend beyond the areas directly cleared or drained: even untouched forest close to degraded areas will have lost some of its natural fire resistance. The El Niño-driven drought has supercharged these changes, making it easier for fires to take hold and spread.
The hidden cost of peat fires

Fire is widely used across the region, to help prepare land for agriculture, clear low-lying vegetation, or to burn household waste. Yet, when fires are set during a drought, they can ignite the drained peatland soil and escape into the surrounding landscape.

A peat fire does not simply flame and pass; it also smoulders downwards into the ground, sometimes burning for weeks or months. An alarming consequence of peat fires is the release of ancient carbon—organic matter that has been safely locked away for hundreds of years. This carbon generally won’t be reabsorbed by future forest growth, as the land has been repurposed for agriculture. It is a permanent transfer of carbon from land into the air.

This year alone, Indonesia’s fires have released an estimated 175 million tonnes of carbon, equivalent to three-quarters of the country’s annual fossil-fuel CO₂ emissions and exceeding the combined annual fossil-fuel and industrial CO₂ emissions of the UK and France.

The scale of the 2026 fire and haze marks a setback after some years of progress. There has been a promising downward trend in regional fire activity, due in part to improved fire management and efforts at “re-wetting” peatlands to make them less flammable.

The severity of the current El Niño has interrupted this good work. Satellite analysis indicates more than 120,000 fire hotspot detections across Indonesia so far – fewer than in 2015 (another El Niño year), but seven times as many as in 2025.

The human and economic cost of the resulting haze is staggering, and many will likely perish from the effects of the toxic smoke. The haze has also drifted beyond Indonesia, at times blanketing neighbouring Malaysia, Brunei, southern Thailand and Singapore.

The health effects of wildfire smoke extend around the world. Globally, exposure contributes to a million or more premature deaths each year, including almost one in ten deaths of children under five.
From detection to prevention

Worryingly, the number of fires in Indonesia could actually be underestimated as satellites are less effective at detecting the lower temperatures of smouldering peat fires. New technologies designed to better detect these fires could help authorities identify them sooner and respond more quickly, provided the data can be rapidly delivered to those who need it.

But better detection and fire suppression can only do so much. In many areas, the key action is to restore drained peatlands so they are less vulnerable to fire in the first place. A new national peatland and mangrove management agency is being established with this remit.

For now, the immediate prognosis remains bleak. It is hard to extinguish underground peat fires once they have taken hold, and the 2026 El Niño is projected to intensify until the end of the year. The immediate crisis will eventually end, but reducing the risk of future disasters will require Indonesia to restore and protect its peatlands with renewed vigour.

articles.title: The greenest initiatives are often the most invisible – experts explain why that’s a problem
articles.author: Diletta Acuti, Senior Lecturer in Marketing, University of Bath
paras: When a company wants to be more sustainable, adding an eco-friendly feature isn’t always better than taking something away.
People often favour “more”. Studies suggest that statements framed around “more” are easier to process and remember than those framed around “less”.

In experiments that involved modifying Lego structures, redesigning miniature golf courses and improving digital grids, it was found that participants routinely overlooked opportunities to improve outcomes through subtraction. People tended to add things rather than remove them, even when subtraction would work better. Recent consumption trends also show this tendency: the size of the average car is growing at a rate of 1cm every two years as larger models have become more popular.

One reason why people favour more is that additions are visible. When people judge a service or a product, they tend to focus on what is in front of them and overlook what is missing. It is easier to notice something a company has added than to value what it has deliberately removed.

That can distort how consumers judge sustainability. A hotel room with bamboo toiletries, a recycled plastic water bottle and other eco-friendly extras may look greener than a room with fewer items, even if removing unnecessary products means less waste. This tendency is known as the sustainable additive bias: people perceive environmentally friendly additions more favourably than reductions, even when reducing use or waste may bring greater environmental benefits.

This bias occurs because visible eco-friendly additions can signal that a company is making an effort and is committed to sustainability. A reduction leaves fewer obvious eco-friendly cues, so consumers may interpret it as “less effort” rather than as a considered attempt to reduce environmental harm.

We tested this bias across nine studies in different product and service settings in our latest study. In an experiment with 302 hotel guests, rooms with more eco-friendly amenities were judged more sustainable than rooms with fewer. Yet guests in those rooms generated a higher proportion of waste. Across the studies, consumers could recognise the benefits of removing conventional, less sustainable items. The bias arose when they compared adding and removing items presented as eco-friendly.

Why is this problematic? When hotels replace single-use toiletries with refillable dispensers, or companies remove unnecessary items from product bundles to cut waste, they may expect consumers to hail these changes as environmentally responsible. But the opposite may happen. Companies that genuinely want to reduce their impact on the environment may be misjudged.

This does not mean companies should avoid replacing less sustainable products with more sustainable alternatives. The concern is adding eco-friendly items that are unnecessary. Companies should explain why reducing these items benefits the environment, so customers do not mistake using less for making less effort.
So sustainable consumption needs a rethink and a cultural change.

Companies should explain why less is more and make the work behind those decisions prominent, explaining the environmental logic: which items or resources are being reduced, why they are unnecessary, and how the change cuts waste or environmental impact.

A food delivery company, for example, could stop automatically including disposable bamboo cutlery and napkins with every order, and instead let consumers request them when needed. The company could explain that it changed its ordering and packing process to avoid sending items many consumers do not use, reducing unnecessary material without changing the meal itself. This helps consumers recognise the effort behind a reduction rather than interpreting it as a lower quality offer or a lack of commitment.

Italian circular-fashion brand Rifó offers an example of making reduction visible: its sustainability report explains how its pre-order model is designed to match production with demand and avoid making garments customers do not need. They also encourage consumers to repair rather than replace with new items.

By emphasising the effectiveness of simple solutions, policymakers can celebrate reduction as a virtue. They can showcase production and consumption practices that use fewer resources, offer fewer unnecessary items or prevent waste – thereby reducing their environmental impact. This approach may benefit consumers too: reducing consumption and materialism can improve people’s wellbeing, while minimalism enhances happiness and life satisfaction. Giving positive examples a visible platform can help challenge the assumption that progress always means adding another product or feature.

Sustainable production alone cannot solve the problem of overconsumption. We need to learn that less can be better. We are accustomed to seeing addition as improvement, but removing what is unnecessary does not mean reducing quality. Sometimes it creates a more efficient service and a genuinely better environmental outcome.

articles.title: Embrace lazy autumn gardening to protect wildlife
articles.author: Kat Hamill, Senior Lecturer in Zoology, Nottingham Trent University
paras: As winter approaches, many of us start clearing leaves and tidying up our gardens. But these jobs can remove vital winter habitats for wildlife, particularly with increasingly volatile weather conditions.

Residential gardens cover 4.6% of Great Britain’s land area – over three times the size of the UK’s National Nature Reserves – so they are important refuges for our biodiversity, particularly in urban areas.
There are many things you can do to make your garden wildlife-friendly, from installing a pond to establishing a compost heap or planting native, flowering plants and trees.

However, research has shown that there are obstacles to householders engaging in wildlife-friendly gardening practices, such as costs and the level of effort or knowledge involved. The effort needed to maintain a garden appears to discourage people to such an extent that almost half (42%) of residential gardens in the UK are now paved over. It even appears a growing number would prefer to cover their gardens in plastic artificial grass rather than (heaven forbid) have an unkempt lawn.

Whether you’re motivated by the thought of encouraging more butterflies into your garden next year or just more time curled up on the sofa, wildlife-friendly gardening can involve less effort. Here is my argument for why you should do less in the garden this autumn.

Leave some leaf litter, raked into a pile in a quiet corner for hedgehogs to use as nesting material for hibernation. Beetles, spiders, and other invertebrates will also shelter in leaf litter – in turn, providing food for foraging birds like robins and blackbirds.

However, leaf litter doesn’t only provide shelter or hunting ground – it can also be an important food source itself. Detritivores, such as woodlice and millipedes, feed on decomposing plant matter and, in doing so, play a crucial role in nutrient cycling.
Dedicate a patch to fallen twigs or a log pile.

Stacking logs creates nooks and crannies, with the centre and bottom of the pile staying wetter and rotting quicker while the top dries out. Although this does involve leaving the warm embrace of the living room, it could give you an easy place to abandon those leftover wood cuts and sweep loose twigs into.

The damp conditions in a log pile are ideal for beetles and woodlice, while ladybirds and butterflies tend to occupy the drier parts. These invertebrates then act as prey for other species, such as amphibians, small mammals, and birds. In this way, a log pile provides a variety of niches, offering refuge and food for a whole wildlife community.
Deadwood habitats are also vital for Europe’s largest beetle: the stag beetle. They spend most of their life as a grub, feeding on rotten wood for several years, before emerging as an adult.

Finding cover as the temperature falls is particularly important for ectotherms, such as amphibians and reptiles, which rely on their surroundings to regulate their body temperature. Frogs, toads, newts, and lizards hide away under log piles, rocks, and vegetation – entering a state of dormancy known as brumation, which is similar to hibernation in mammals.

Hang fire on deadheading spent flowers and cutting back perennial stems until the following spring. The seed heads are an important food source for birds, such as sparrows and finches, as well as small mammals like mice and voles. The hollow stems also provide shelter for solitary bees.

If you’re lucky enough to have a fruit tree in your garden, spare a few windfalls. Fallen apples and pears will be eaten by mammals, from small rodents through to badgers, and birds, like thrushes and tits. They are also a late-season source of sugar for butterflies, ants, and other invertebrates.

Resist the urge to tidy the garden on the first sunny day of spring. Many animals only emerge from dormancy once the days start to get longer or temperatures consistently rise. Early gardening may expose over-wintering wildlife to late-season frosts. This could also include delaying mowing the lawn, to leave the dandelions and clover as an early source of nectar for bees.

By simply doing less, we can promote habitat complexity and help increase species diversity in our gardens. So, we should embrace a “messy” garden as the new norm – and feel a little less guilty if we don’t get around to ticking the gardening off our weekend chore list.

articles.title: 50 years later, Amory Lovins’ soft energy path meets electrification
articles.author: Daniel Cohan, Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Rice University
paras: Hurricane Belle was barreling toward New England in August 1976 when an editor from Foreign Affairs called. Physicist Amory Lovins took the call on a payphone in a shack in the Maine woods, where he spent summers as a camp guide.

“If it happened to hit that area, the wires would be down with trees on them for weeks, so we’d miss the press date,” Lovins told me in a 2025 interview. The lines held up as he and the editor worked through final edits on a 14-hour phone call.
Published in October 1976 in the wake of the 1973 oil crisis, “Energy Strategy: The Road Not Taken?” drew more reprint requests than any Foreign Affairs article in decades.

Two U.S. Senate committees called on the 29-year-old Lovins to testify about his ideas that December. The following year, Lovins met with President Jimmy Carter and his top energy advisers in the Oval Office and expanded his article into a book, “Soft Energy Paths: Toward a Durable Peace.” The New York Times chronicled the “raging debate” sparked by Lovins, noting that “even his critics concede that he is something of a genius.”

The article charted two paths for the future of energy. One, which Lovins called the “hard” path, required ever more energy supply to meet inexorably rising demand. With U.S. oil production in decline since 1970, coal and uranium would supply most growth by generating electricity at large, remote facilities.

Lovins instead championed a “soft” path that put people’s wants ahead of supplies. “People do not want electricity or oil … but rather comfortable rooms, light, vehicular motion … and other real things,” he wrote.

The soft path would meet those wants with a diverse array of renewable energy resources, sourced locally where possible. Heating would come from solar collectors and waste heat. Vehicles would be made more efficient and run on biofuels. Wind power would be used to compress air to drive machinery. Oil and gas would be reserved for making chemicals. Lovins hoped that matching form with function could enable U.S. energy use to plateau and then decline so that it could be supplied renewably by 2025.

When Lovins wrote his article, most electricity was generated inefficiently from fossil fuels or uranium, while wind and solar power remained prohibitively expensive. “Photovoltaics were out of bounds intellectually; that gets you laughed out of the room, and I didn’t actually think they would get cheap enough,” Lovins told me in 2025.

Burning or fissioning a fuel to generate electricity inefficiently, transmitting it far away, and turning it back into low-grade heat for homes was “like cutting butter with a chainsaw,” Lovins wrote. Thus, his soft path included only a narrowing lane for electricity, steering it toward essential purposes such as electronics, subways, lighting and smelting. Lovins posited that “an affluent industrial economy could advantageously operate with no central power stations at all,” though he did not advocate going that far.

They were paths, not predictions, and neither path foretold the road actually taken in the 50 years since. Unlike most forecasts from the era, which projected ever-rising demand, the soft path foresaw that total U.S. energy use could plateau, and it almost exactly matched the actual level in 2000. However, Lovins and his contemporaries failed to foresee the drilling advances that have kept oil and gas dominant.

As an environmental engineer completing a book about the visions that are shaping energy realities and opportunities around the world, I think Lovins got it half right about how to secure sustainable energy. Efficiency and renewable energy are indeed essential, but clean electricity and electrification are proving far more important than Lovins expected.

Critics argued that Lovins underestimated the costs of clean technologies and overstated what they could achieve. In fact, opportunities for clean energy have been transformed by unanticipated plunges in the costs of wind and solar electricity, battery storage and LED lighting.

For example, the price per watt of solar panels tumbled from around US$100 in current dollars in 1976 to around 10 cents in global markets today and a President Donald Trump-set minimum price of 38 cents for panels imported to the United States.
The soft path goes electric

Modern technologies turn the chainsaw analogy on its head by making electrification the soft path to reducing energy use. Heat pumps supply several times as much heat as the electricity they consume. Induction stoves cook food far more efficiently than gas flames. And electric vehicles are a few times more efficient than gasoline ones.

Powered by renewable electricity, from local resources like the solar panels on Lovins’ roof and mine, or from larger solar, wind and geothermal facilities, these technologies can slash fossil fuel use. A diversity of resources blended with high-voltage transmission and storage can make clean electricity available around the clock.

When I visited Lovins’ ultra-efficient, solar-powered Colorado home in 2025, electrification took center stage. It was the induction stove that he showed off first, boiling water at lightning speed, then the batteries in the utility room. Two electric cars were charging outside. The wood stoves had been retired.

Former colleagues of Lovins now advocate an “electrotech revolution” centered on renewable electricity and increased electrification. Lovins told me he embraces their work but is pushing them to add integrative design — optimizing efficiency by redesigning whole systems — a subject he teaches at Stanford.
I believe Lovins was right to focus on matching resources with people’s actual needs. Renewable electrification and efficiency provide the softest path to doing so for the next 50 years.
Daniel Cohan interviewed Amory Lovins three times while writing two books.

articles.title: Robert Eggers’s Werwulf: the real history of wolves and werewolves in medieval England
articles.author: Aleks Pluskowski, Professor of Medieval Archaeology, University of Reading
paras: Robert Eggers’s historical folk horror Werwulf will be in cinemas this winter. It’s set in 1305, when wolves still roamed parts of England. As they vanished from English shores due to sustained hunting, however, the werewolf myth moved abroad. The creature changed from a pitiable victim into a diabolical killer, before being rediscovered and reinvented by the Victorians.

In Eggers’s film, a hunter arrives in an English village to enlist local peasants in a wolf hunt declared by the king. The premise has a real historical basis, as the character appears to be inspired by Peter Corbet, a Shropshire baron of the Welsh Marches.

In 1281, Corbet was commissioned by Edward I to hunt and destroy all wolves within a cluster of counties bordering Wales, with the aid of the king’s bailiffs. Although the campaign is sometimes explained as an effort to protect England’s lucrative wool industry, Edward’s orders specified the crown’s hunting domains first and foremost. Surviving documentation from medieval Britain often places wolves within forests, chases and parks, where populations of deer were also concentrated.

The wolf population in Britain endured Corbet’s hunts, although the last ones are difficult to pin down. Young individuals could have dispersed into already “cleared” areas, and a pack was almost certainly present on the North York Moors at the end of the 14th century. It is thought they may also have lingered in the Scottish Highlands into the 18th century. Animal remains currently being investigated may yet help archaeologists refine that timeline.

Early on in Werwulf, one of the farmers enlisted in the wolf hunt turns out to be a werewolf. Medieval people did believe in this possibility. In his encyclopedic work Otia Imperialia (Recreation for an Emperor), published in 1211, the statesman and writer Gervase of Tilbury described men transforming into wolves in England in accordance with the phases of the moon.

Gervase presented this as a real occurrence, but there were also accounts of fictional werewolves. Texts circulating in England such as poet Marie de France’s Bisclavret (circa 1160-1175) and the French folk romance, Guillaume de Palerne (William of Palerne), from around 1350, show werewolves being incorporated into courtly storytelling.
These texts told tales of human nobles trapped in wolf form, more victims than monsters. Yet they drew their imaginative power from landscapes in which real wolves could be seen and heard.
From pitiable victim to devil’s agent

Wolves continued to be written about in negative terms long after their disappearance, while werewolves became increasingly associated with foreign lands. But werewolves were also changing character, from victims of misfortune to agents of Satan.

In 1590, a pamphlet was printed in London which described the life, trial and brutal execution of Peter Stumpp, a German man accused of being a werewolf. Stumpp, a farmer from Bedburg near Cologne, had allegedly made a pact with the devil and acquired a magical belt that enabled him to assume the form of a wolf. The pamphlet was translated and expanded from the German account by the writer George Bores.

Stump was not presented as a sympathetic human trapped in wolf form, but as a murderous sorcerer who killed people and livestock and committed sexual violence, incest and cannibalism. Foreign werewolves were not entirely new. The 12th-century writer Gerald of Wales had placed his compassionate werewolves in Ireland, but Stumpp’s diabolical werewolf was a different creature entirely.

The English pamphlet significantly expanded and sensationalised the account it was based on, resulting in a 21-page narrative with an eight-panel woodcut image showing Stumpp’s capture, trial and execution. It also went to considerable lengths to establish the credibility of its story, invoking witnesses and correspondence from Germany.
Stumpp’s case was one of at least 300 prosecutions of werewolfery which formed an occasional component of the much larger number of witchcraft trials in early modern Europe.

In Britain, wolves were not sufficiently embedded in everyday life to become part of witchcraft prosecutions. In Scotland, however, with its intense witch-hunting culture and a surviving wolf population, a 17th-century court record shows the term being used as an insult, although there were no prosecutions of werewolves. In this respect the presence of wolves alone cannot explain where such accusations arose.
Rediscovering the werewolf
With the end of witch hunting, the werewolf largely disappeared from Britain as a serious supernatural possibility.

Then in the 19th century, writers and antiquarians began recovering and reinventing werewolf lore as part of a wider fascination with the Middle Ages. Priest and hagiographer Sabine Baring-Gould’s Book of Were-Wolves (1865) is the best example of this process. He consolidated a huge body of werewolf lore for English-speaking readers, helping to establish the comparative tradition for later popular representations.

Hollywood later drew on this inheritance, but made the werewolf a sympathetic cursed victim again in The Wolf Man (1941), a figure closer to Bisclavret than to Stumpp. In his upcoming film, Eggers has claimed he has hit the reset button on the werewolf, presenting the story of a cursed man seeking salvation through love, a premise that also echoes the werewolves of medieval courtly literature.
Meanwhile, wolves are recolonising parts of continental Europe. There is also an ongoing discussion about their reintroduction to Britain.

What will happen if wolves return as free-living animals after centuries of imagining them through stories? Today we do not fear literal shape changers stalking our forests and moorlands. Yet popular culture gives animals enduring meanings. Just look at the influence of Little Red Riding Hood and the persistent “big bad wolf”.
Werwulf could be the next story to shape how we imagine wolves. If they do return, those meanings may influence how we live with them.

articles.title: Daylight saving was meant to save energy. Do we still need it in the age of LEDs?
articles.author: Amin Al-Habaibeh, Professor of Intelligent Engineering Systems, Nottingham Trent University
paras: When the clocks go back each October, we gain an hour of sleep and lose an hour of evening daylight. The practice of moving the clocks forward in spring was introduced partly to save energy, by making better use of daylight at the end of the day so there would be less need for artificial lighting.

But the lights in our homes have changed dramatically since the UK first adopted summer time in 1916 – and the change over the past decade or so has been especially rapid. A modern LED bulb can produce as much light as an old-fashioned 100-watt bulb while using a fraction of the electricity. This raises a question: in an age of energy-efficient lighting, does changing the clocks still save us much energy?

The UK introduced the clock change in 1916, during the first world war, to conserve fuel and enhance productivity. Moving the clock one hour forward would delay sunset relative to the time, and hence should save energy by reducing the need for lights after dark.

After a few tweaks in the 1960s and 70s, the current scheme has been in place since 1980, with clocks going forward on the last Sunday in March and reverting to Greenwich Mean Time on the last Sunday in October. Since the mid-1990s, these dates have been harmonised across the EU to reduce any disruption in travel and business.

But whether the clock change delivers the energy savings originally intended remains uncertain. A 2026 House of Commons Library report found that the effects of clock changes on energy demand are inconclusive. The potential savings from reduced lighting use can be offset by changes in heating and cooling demand.
Modern lights use a lot less electricity

Incandescent bulbs, which produce light by passing an electric current through a tungsten filament, are highly inefficient. Most of their energy goes into generating heat – of the electricity they consume, just 5% to 10% or so is turned into light. These bulbs were phased out of the UK market between 2009 and 2012, followed by most halogen bulbs (a similar technology) in 2021.

Those bulbs were replaced by light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, now the most efficient light bulbs in widespread use. An LED bulb producing the same amount of light as a 100-watt incandescent bulb (about 1,520 lumens) would use just 13.5 watts – an electricity saving of around 86%. Almost every light you see today is based on LED technology.

This means that producing a given amount of artificial light now requires much less electricity than it did when daylight saving time was introduced. But that doesn’t, by itself, tell us how much energy changing the clocks saves today.

Lighting has historically been only a small percentage of household energy consumption. Today, it accounts for about 4% of household electricity consumption in the UK, or about 1% of overall household energy use (which includes gas for heating), according to government estimates for 2025. However, overall household energy consumption has in general declined since the 2000s, mainly due to the adoption of other energy-efficient measures.

More efficient lighting can also change how people use it. Lower running costs may encourage people to use more lights, especially for decoration, or to leave them on for longer – economists call this a rebound effect.
That’s why we can’t only look at how efficient light bulbs have become. We have to consider how much electricity the clock change saves across the energy system as a whole.
Only modest energy savings – at best
Modern life is significantly different from when the clock change was introduced in 1916. We have renewable energy, electric cars, and homes and offices packed with electronic and computer equipment.

A study from 2018 that combined 162 estimates from 44 studies found average energy savings of about 0.34% during daylight saving time. A further study from 2025 suggests that the original justification for daylight saving time as an energy-saving measure is increasingly uncertain. Broadly, research suggests reductions in lighting demand are most likely to be balanced by increased heating and cooling demand. Any energy savings are likely to be relatively small and depend on factors beyond lighting efficiency.

The European Parliament voted in 2019 to abolish the twice-yearly clock change, although implementation has stalled because EU countries have not agreed whether to keep permanent summer or winter time.

The move from incandescent bulbs to LEDs has hugely reduced the electricity needed for lighting, weakening one of the original reasons for changing the clocks. But the available research does not offer a simple calculation of how much energy the UK or similar countries would save or use if the system was abandoned.

The original rationale was straightforward: shift daylight into the evening hours and reduce the need for electrical lights. Today, much more efficient bulbs mean that the potential savings from clock changes are smaller than they once were. Whether that makes daylight saving unnecessary depends on the wider effects of changing our clocks – and the evidence on those effects remains inconclusive.

articles.title: 18 million people living in poverty depend on underwater meadows for food and income - but these vital habitats are under threat
articles.author: Richard K.F. Unsworth, Associate Professor in Marine Biology, Swansea University
paras: At least 18 million people living in poverty across the Indo-Pacific fish in seagrass meadows, while around 6.5 million rely on them as their only fishing grounds. For these communities, the underwater habitats are not simply part of the natural environment but a source of food and a means of earning a living.

But these important fishing grounds face growing pressure from coastal development, changes in land use and poor water quality. When seagrass meadows are damaged or lost, the consequences can extend beyond wildlife. The fish and other marine life they support may also be affected, putting food supplies and household incomes at risk.

Our latest research examines the scale of this dependence and how it relates to poverty. The findings highlight a question that conservation efforts need to address: what happens to people whose livelihoods depend on habitats that are under growing pressure?

Seagrasses are flowering plants that grow in shallow coastal waters. They form underwater meadows that support fish and other marine life. People can fish in these habitats using simple nets, traps and lines, or collect shellfish and other marine animals by hand. Unlike some other fishing grounds, seagrass meadows can often be reached without a boat or expensive equipment.

This level of accessibility can be particularly important for households with few resources or alternative ways to earn money. Yet seagrass conservation is often discussed in terms of protecting wildlife and storing carbon. We have known that these habitats support fisheries, but we have had much less understanding of how many people living in poverty rely on them.
To investigate this, we analysed data from nearly 2,000 households in more than 150 coastal communities across Cambodia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Sri Lanka and Tanzania.

We looked at household incomes, fishing activities and the habitats people used to catch fish and collect other marine resources. We then compared the livelihoods of households using different fishing grounds, including those living in poverty.

More than 80% of households in the communities we studied were involved in fishing, either to earn money, provide food or both. Households that relied entirely on seagrass fisheries earned around 23% less than those fishing in other habitats, even after we accounted for differences in household size.

To put this in perspective, if a household earns £7.50 per day, a 23% difference amounts to roughly £52 a month. For a family already struggling to afford food, healthcare or education, this is a substantial amount of money.

The dependence was especially striking among households living in extreme poverty. Almost half fished in seagrass as well as other habitats, while more than a 25% relied on seagrass alone. This does not mean that seagrass fishing causes poverty. Rather, accessible fishing grounds may be particularly important to people who cannot afford a boat or specialist equipment.

We then combined our household data with estimates of how many people live near seagrass meadows. Across the five countries we studied, we estimate that 10.8 million people living in poverty use seagrass for fishing. Around 5.4 million may rely on it as their only fishing habitat.

The stakes go beyond income. In separate research published earlier this year, we found that fish communities associated with seagrass could provide a wider range of essential nutrients than those associated with coral reefs. Although reefs supported more fish overall, seagrass fish communities had greater potential to supply several important nutrients together.

These include iron, which helps prevent anaemia, zinc, which supports children’s growth and immune systems, calcium, which is essential for health bones, and omega-3 fatty acids which support brain development. For families that cannot afford a varied diet, fish, even as a soup or broth, can provide several of these nutrients in a single meal. Losing access to seagrass could therefore not only mean losing income, but also a vital source of nutrition, especially for children and vulnerable family members.

These risks are important considerations because seagrass meadows face pressure globally. Research suggests that around 20% of surveyed seagrass meadow area in the Indo-Pacific has been lost over the past 70 to 90 years, with coastal development and declining water quality among the major threats identified.

Elsewhere in the Indo-Pacific, researchers documented an 84% decline in fish abundance following substantial seagrass loss. For coastal families that depend on these habitats, this means fewer fish available to catch, fewer income opportunities and less food.
Protecting seagrass means protecting people

Protecting these habitats, however, is not as simple as restricting fishing. Conservation measures that limit access to fishing grounds could harm communities if they depend on them for food or income and have few alternatives. At the same time, local fishers may have little control over other sources of damage, such as pollution from agriculture or development along the coast.

Conservation plans therefore need to consider both the health of seagrass meadows and the people who depend on them. Where restrictions on fishing are proposed, decision-makers should assess the probable effects on local incomes and food supplies. They should also consider whether realistic alternatives are available and address damage caused by pollution and coastal development, rather than placing the burden of conservation on fishing communities alone.

In the Philippines, local fishing communities are already helping manage marine reserves that protect seagrass meadows. Some approaches allow fishing and shellfish collection to continue while restricting more damaging activities or protecting smaller areas where marine life can recover.

In Indonesia, years of forest clearance had increased soil erosion, washing sediment into coastal waters and threatening seagrass meadows. In response, local governments, communities and organisations came together to plant more than 4,500 trees along riverbanks to reduce the amount of sediment entering the sea and protecting the seagrass fishing grounds that local families depend on.

Protecting seagrass will not solve coastal poverty on its own, however. But our findings show why conservation policies need to recognise the people who depend on these habitats. Safeguarding seagrass means protecting not only marine life but also an important source of food and income for millions of people.
