articles.title: Greener maternity care starts with changing hospitals, without putting pressure on pregnant women
articles.author: Alice Craggs, Lecturer in Midwifery, School of Nursing and Midwifery, London South Bank University
paras: The NHS has a substantial carbon footprint. Yet one part of its environmental impact receives relatively little attention: maternity care.

The health service is responsible for an estimated 4% to 5% of England’s greenhouse gas emissions. A 2025 report from the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists estimated that selected maternity care activities in England generated about 205,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in 2022–23.

CO₂e expresses the warming effect of different greenhouse gases, such as methane, as an equivalent amount of carbon dioxide. The analysis excluded some maternity services, so the total footprint is likely to be higher.

Nearly 29% of the emissions across the activities studied came from Entonox, commonly known as gas and air. It contains nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas. Using it during regular contractions over four hours has an estimated warming effect of 237kg CO₂e.

Travel to appointments also contributes to emissions. An analysis at the Whittington, a hospital in north London, estimated that a patient’s return journey to an antenatal appointment generated an average of 1.23kg CO₂e.
Hospitals also use large quantities of disposable equipment. Ready-to-use formula bottles and teats, single-use cups and clinical waste containers are routinely used once and discarded.

Pregnancy is sometimes described as a “teachable moment”, when people may be particularly receptive to health information. Environmental advice could become part of those conversations, including discussions about feeding a baby or choosing pain relief.
Responsibility for reducing emissions

But placing responsibility on parents creates ethical problems. Maternity care in the UK is already under intense pressure. The 2022 Ockenden review documented serious failures in maternity safety, while the 2024 birth trauma inquiry highlighted how women’s concerns were dismissed or ignored.
Against that background, asking someone in labour to weigh the climate effects of pain relief alongside their comfort and safety could create another burden at an already demanding time.

Measuring emissions can help hospitals improve how services are designed. But carbon targets should not be used to restrict access to caesarean birth or pain relief. Decisions about care should respect each person’s needs and informed choices.

In a small interview study involving 12 people who had used nitrous oxide during labour, most wanted environmental information to be available during pregnancy. However, they were unsure whether knowing its impact would change their choice of pain relief. Participants also considered reducing emissions to be primarily the responsibility of healthcare organisations.
A more useful approach is to change how maternity services are delivered while protecting patient choice.

Some NHS maternity services are already doing this. At Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals, a project introduced virtual ward support and care at home for patients with severe pregnancy sickness. By reducing hospital stays, it cut emissions by an estimated 538kg CO₂e over one month. The team projected an annual saving of around 6,462kg if those reductions continued.

Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust has introduced technology that captures exhaled gas and air and breaks down the nitrous oxide into nitrogen and oxygen, allowing women to continue using gas and air during labour while reducing its environmental impact.

Other changes involve purchasing and waste. Thousands of ready-to-use plastic formula bottles and teats are used in maternity care. A 2019 letter from Irish researchers published in the British Medical Journal highlighted waste from unconsumed formula and discarded packaging. Reducing this could lower emissions without restricting access to formula for those who need or choose it.

Similar questions apply to disposable products throughout maternity wards. Clinicians work in systems designed around single-use equipment and established waste procedures. Changing those systems is likely to be more effective than expecting individual clinicians to improvise greener alternatives.
At the midwife-led White Horse birth centre in Swindon, staff have replaced plastic containers used to dispose of placentas with alternatives made from 96% paper, reducing plastic use and costs.

Breastfeeding illustrates how complicated individual responsibility can become. Compared with exclusive formula feeding, exclusive breastfeeding for six months has been estimated to have a carbon footprint 95kg to 153kg CO₂e lower per baby.

But feeding decisions depend on health and personal circumstances, including the support available to parents. A more useful approach would be to provide effective support for anyone who wants to breastfeed, while reducing unnecessary waste and emissions from the way formula is purchased, prepared and supplied by maternity services.
Better care, lower emissions

The Green Maternity Challenge, part of a programme led by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, brought together nine NHS teams to test ways of reducing emissions while improving maternity care. Several projects involved redesigning services to make treatment easier to access or reduce unnecessary hospital stays.

Better care and lower emissions can go together. But treating sustainability only as a fortunate side effect risks overlooking opportunities to design maternity services deliberately around lower-carbon care.

Hospitals should examine where their emissions come from and give staff the knowledge and resources to reduce them. Changes to purchasing and waste systems, alongside suitable lower-emission technologies, can help services become greener while protecting safe care and informed choice.

Childbirth will always carry an environmental footprint. Health services have the responsibility and practical means to reduce the impact through changes to how care is organised and delivered. Those changes should protect choices without placing additional burdens on the person giving birth.

articles.title: How El Niño could push up your mortgage and grocery bills
articles.author: Narmin Nahidi, Assistant Professor in Finance, University of Exeter
paras: This year’s El Niño, the natural weather phenomenon that drives variations in temperature and winds across the Pacific, has prompted the UK government to pledge £15 million to help vulnerable countries such as Malawi, Kenya and Zambia prepare for droughts, floods and food shortages.
But the UK’s economic response will go beyond international aid. The Bank of England has identified El Niño as one of the key factors that could increase food inflation in 2027.

This connection between a climate pattern in the Pacific Ocean and supermarket prices (and possibly interest rates) in the UK is a clear demonstration of how extreme weather is an economic issue as well as an environmental one.

Environmentally speaking, the effects of El Niño can be devastating, bringing severe drought to some regions and severe flooding to others. And a stronger El Niño has a larger influence on global weather patterns than a weaker one.

This year’s event, already the strongest on record, is expected to peak later this year, and could cause global economic problems if it has a negative effect on major agricultural producers or transport routes.
Poor harvests can cause international agricultural prices to rise. Higher energy costs can simultaneously make fertiliser, processing and transportation more expensive.
The UK is particularly exposed to climate-related disruptions because of the international nature of its food supply (about 42% of its food is imported).

But these effects are rarely immediate. Many food manufacturers and retailers use risk management techniques to limit their exposure to sudden changes in prices, which can initially shield consumers from international shocks.
The Bank of England made this point explicitly, saying the potential effects of El Niño are likely to emerge gradually, rather than causing widespread food shortages or dramatic price rises.
And the central bank of Spain found that the effect of El Niño varies according to commodity, time period and agricultural policy.

For the most part, disasters with regard to food supply can be avoided with the right kind of human intervention. Businesses adapt. Farmers change production decisions. Trade shifts towards alternative suppliers. Governments intervene.
El Niño should therefore be viewed as a potential source of risk and volatility, rather than as a confident prediction that UK food prices must rise.
But what happens when several external shocks occur together?
The Bank of England has considered this possibility too, warning that a strong El Niño alongside renewed energy disruption could put much greater pressure on UK food prices.

If extreme weather also affects major shipping routes, the effects on import prices could become stronger still. This is where a climate event potentially becomes a monetary policy problem, as central banks treat El Niño as a factor that may cause them to raise interest rates.

In a recent meeting, the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee identified severe El Niño conditions as one possible source of additional pressure on agricultural prices, alongside energy markets and other global supply risks.

And this perhaps explains the thinking behind the UK government’s plan to help countries prepare for El Niño. The £15 million pledge announced in September 2026 is based on the idea of “anticipatory action”: releasing money before a predictable emergency rather than waiting until the economic damage has occurred.
The government says around 35% of humanitarian shocks can be predicted in advance, while less than 1% of global humanitarian funding currently goes towards anticipatory action.
There is a broader financial principle at work here.
If climate forecasts contain economically useful information, financial decisions can respond before losses actually occur.

So food importers can reconsider commodity and currency strategies to guard against shocks. Banks can incorporate weather-related supply disruption into their financial evaluations, and companies can stress-test supply chains against simultaneous commodity, energy and transportation shocks.
Governments can connect climate forecasting more closely with food security and planning for economic resilience.

And while they may not be able to predict exactly what El Niño will do to the price of a shopping basket, they can certainly act in a way that recognises the fact that information about future weather has financial value.

The UK government has shown that it is using weather forecasts to release humanitarian finance before disasters happen overseas. Those forecasts no longer provide key information just for meteorologists, farmers and fishing boats.
Increasingly, they contain vital financial data.

articles.title: As flood risk rises, some communities question the idea of resilience
articles.author: Paul O'Hare, Lecturer in Human Geography and Urban Development, Manchester Metropolitan University
paras: Climate change is increasing flood risk across the UK. As floods become more frequent and intense, communities are increasingly encouraged to become resilient and “live with water”. Yet in some flood-prone areas, residents are rejecting these calls, concerned that resilience is less about helping communities and more about transferring responsibility from institutions to citizens.

Resilience is often considered to be a positive idea. It suggests that people can adapt to uncertainty, to prepare for disruption, and recover quickly when floods strike. But my research suggests many communities are deeply uncomfortable with this messaging. Some reject it altogether.
My research with three flood action groups in north-west England drew on 17 semi-structured interviews and extensive participant observation over a five-year period.
One resident told me rather bluntly: “Resilience offers hope. But for me it’s false hope. A way of telling people, you’ll flood. What are you going to do about it?”

Debates about resilience reveal more fundamental concerns: who should bear responsibility for managing the consequences of climate change? And how much can reasonably be expected of citizens and communities?

For much of the 20th century, flood management was dominated by efforts to protect people and property through engineered defences, embankments and complex drainage systems. Though this approach continues to this day, governments and policymakers now also encourage people to “live with water”, accepting that some degree of flooding is inevitable. Property owners are advised to install flood doors, change flooring and fit water-resilient furniture and kitchens. They’re also encouraged to sign up for warnings, arrange adequate insurance cover and develop action plans for when the waters rise.
On the surface, this seems sensible. Who would not want communities that can recover quickly from disasters? Yet it can sit uncomfortably with many of those expected to become more resilient.

Many participants in our research expressed concern that resilience agendas shifted responsibility away from institutions onto communities. Several people I spoke to rejected the language of resilience because it implied they should adapt to repeated flooding and recover independently. As one participant reflected: “Resilience? It’s safe to say I’m not a fan. It’s all about you (pointing a finger at themselves). You’re the one with the problem.”

Some residents were particularly sceptical about interventions such as property level resilience measures, which have become increasingly important for community flood risk management. Many viewed these measures as sticking plasters rather than solutions to the underlying causes of recurring flood risk. As one flood action group leader explained, “people want to see spades in the ground. They want to see defences going in”.
Resilience is becoming politically contested

Though often presented as a technical solution, resilience has become a source of contestation and debate. Rather than accepting expert advice at face value, many residents challenged authorities, questioned planning decisions, and demanded greater accountability and investment in flood protection.

Such concerns do not occur in a vacuum. Many flood-affected communities have experienced prolonged pressure on public services and local government budgets. Against this context, calls to become more resilient can be interpreted as yet another expectation that communities manage problems that were once addressed collectively.

In particular, many objected to resilience when it appeared a substitute for investment, protection and institutional responsibility. As one interviewee put it: “All these agencies and the council, they’re telling us to be resilient. But what are they doing to help us be resilient and protect us? What are they doing to be resilient themselves?”

Adaptation is essential. But if the notion of resilience is to receive public acceptance, it can’t become a substitute for public investment and institutional accountability. Communities are more likely to embrace resilience when it’s a collaborative effort involving local authorities, agencies and community organisations. Resilience then becomes a shared responsibility, rather than an expectation placed upon residents.
Communities are not rejecting adaptation. But they are questioning approaches that ask them to live with water while feeling increasingly alone in dealing with its consequences.

articles.title: Moths in art history: centuries of creativity reveal the beauty of a misunderstood insect
articles.author: Samuel Shaw, Senior Lecturer in History of Art, The Open University
paras: Moths seem to be made for Halloween. They’re largely nocturnal, often outlandish in appearance and bear creepy names such as Lunar Thorn, Cloaked Carpet, Bordered Gothic and (best of all) Puss Moth.
The webs of the ermine moth caterpillar cover trees like ghostly shrouds, while the hairy caterpillars of the oak processionary moth release rash-inducing toxins.

Spookiest of all is the Death’s-head Hawk-moth, which bears a skull-like mark on its thorax and can squeak like a mouse. This is the moth that appears, albeit in altered form, on the poster for the film The Silence of the Lambs (1991).

Two historical prints held at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam speak to the long-held suspicion of moths within European society. In one work by the printmaker C. Galle, a group sets out with lamps to destroy moths before they can eat the crops (or produce caterpillars that do). In another, by Jan Luyken, women inspect the holes that moths have made in fabric. The Old English origins of the word “moth” denote a primarily destructive, parasitical creature.

Unlike butterflies (who doesn’t like butterflies?) humans have always found moths hard to love. I certainly didn’t give moths much consideration until this year, when I started researching representations of moths and spending time with the moths themselves. I’ve since become something of a moth evangelist.

From March of this year my son and I set up a Skinner moth trap in our small suburban garden in Leicester, rising early every morning to identify the moths that visited during the night. My expectations were low, especially in the first few weeks, when we caught little. But then May and June came, and every morning brought new gifts. My son took charge of the counting and by September we had identified a hundred different species.

If you think moths are all small, brown creatures, think again. Even in the UK, and despite their rapidly decreasing numbers, moths are astonishingly diverse and outstandingly beautiful, ranging widely in size, colour and temperament. Some of them – most famously, the luminously pink and green Elephant Hawk-moth – are disarmingly cute and docile and will happily sit on your hand.

The magic of moths has attracted artists for centuries. A good place to start is the Flemish artist Joris Hoefnagel (1542-1601), whose delicate watercolour sketches of moths remain astonishingly lifelike. I especially like his depiction of the furry Hummingbird Hawk-moth: one of a few day-flying moths and one of a few species benefiting from recent rises in temperature.

Even more astonishing is the work of the pioneering German naturalist and artist Maria Sibylla Merian (1647-1717), who published three books detailing the metamorphosis of butterflies and moths (or what she called “summer-birds” and “moth-birds”). Merian’s elegantly composed images were the first to situate moths within their wider environment, identifying which species preferred which plants.

Outside of the world of natural history, moths have tended to be given a marginal role. However, some artists have been as drawn to moths as moths are drawn to light. In 1959, for example, the Scottish artist John Maxwell (1905-1962) painted a series of colourful, abstracted moth paintings, including Night Flowers and Garden at Night (Moth).

Moths are especially well served by contemporary artists. The Peruvian contemporary artist Lorena Solís Bravo has considered the moth through the lens of queer ecology. Their 2024 film myth, moth, mother celebrates the mystery and transformative power of moths. The Devon-based printmaker Sarah Gillespie, meanwhile, has created a series of mesmerising mezzotint prints of moths. “I wasn’t looking for moths when I started drawing them around ten years ago,” Gillespie has explained “they came and found me. Their numbers may be in appalling decline but for me their presence has become ever more insistent”.

More recently, the artist Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg unveiled The Length of a Moment, three public sculptures at Oxford North, which visualise the flight of a moth interacting with the scent of a flower. Situated in an area rich with historic meadows, this artwork draws attention to diminishing moth populations and the need for better environmental management.

My favourite moth in art, however, comes courtesy of the 18th-century Indian artist Shaikh Zain al–Din. The moth that appears in his 1778 watercolour is the famous Death’s-head Hawk-moth. Here, however, it lacks the sinister and spectral nature of the moth from The Silence of the Lambs. Instead Shaikh Zain al–Din gives us a moth just going about its everyday (or every night?) business.

This isn’t the moth as a symbol of death, or as a muncher of clothes or crops (of the circa 2,500 species of moth found in the UK, only two actually eat clothes). This is a moth doing what moths do well: feeding from and pollinating plants, providing food for birds and looking rather beautiful while doing so. This image is a timely reminder that moths are much less weird and way more wonderful than most people think.
Samuel Shaw has previously received funding from the Arts and Humanities Research Council

articles.title: The Jackdaw gasfield passed the legal test for North Sea drilling – Rosebank will find it much harder
articles.author: Robert Hargreaves, Lecturer in Law, York St John University
paras: For the first time, UK ministers have had to weigh the emissions from burning gas extracted from a North Sea field before approving its development. The way they did so for Jackdaw says a good deal about how the far larger Rosebank oil field is likely to fare.

Coverage of the decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field has focused on energy security and household bills. But the decision also marks an important test of the legal rules governing new fossil fuel projects. Jackdaw, about 150 miles, or 250km, east of Aberdeen, could send gas ashore from as early as the end of October. Yet the project was first approved in 2022, only for a court to strike that approval down. What happened in between explains why the much larger Rosebank oil field will find the same test far harder.

How a government elected on a promise of no new oil and gas licences can approve new drilling turns on a distinction that rarely makes the headlines. A licence gives a company exclusive rights over an area of seabed, but it does not, on its own, allow anything to be built or any oil or gas to be produced. The regulator must also consent to the project, with the energy secretary’s agreement following an environmental impact assessment. Jackdaw had its licence, but lacked a consent that could survive in court.
The case that changed the rules

That process was transformed by a dispute over a modest oil site at Horse Hill in Surrey, where campaigner Sarah Finch argued that the environmental assessment should have counted not only the emissions from drilling but also those released once the oil was refined and burned as fuel. In June 2024 the Supreme Court agreed by a majority of three to two, reasoning that since the whole purpose of extracting oil is to burn it, those emissions are an effect of the project itself. As The Conversation reported at the time, the ruling’s effects were always likely to reach well beyond Surrey.

Jackdaw and Rosebank had both been approved without any such calculation, and in January 2025 the Court of Session in Edinburgh, hearing challenges brought by the campaign groups Greenpeace and Uplift, quashed both approvals. Construction continued, but neither field could produce anything until ministers decided again. After the government published new guidance in June 2025, the developer, Adura, went back to the regulator with fresh information.

The decision document shows those rules at work for the first time. Jackdaw’s total emissions, including those from burning its gas and the liquids produced alongside it, are put at up to 36.6 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over the field’s life, with only about 2% coming from production itself. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, accepted that those emissions are likely to have a significant effect on the environment, and then approved the field anyway.

That is exactly what the Finch ruling allows, since it requires decision makers to face the climate cost openly rather than refuse every project that carries one. Fahnbulleh set what her decision calls “moderate adverse weight” on the emissions against “significant positive weight” for energy security. Because most of Jackdaw’s gas will be burned in the UK, she measured its emissions against the country’s legally binding carbon budgets, of which they would make up no more than 1.32% in any single period, and concluded that they would not stop the UK reaching net zero by 2050.

It is worth stressing, though, that Jackdaw’s approval does not set a precedent that ministers can simply apply to every new field. Each project must still be assessed on its own merits, with its emissions weighed against its claimed benefits. That balance could look very different for Rosebank, an oil field whose output is far less likely to be used in the UK than Jackdaw’s gas.

Greenpeace says the approval shows the “grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over energy policy”, although it has not so far announced a fresh legal challenge. Any challenge would most likely return to the Court of Session, where applications for judicial review normally must be made within three months. Judicial review asks whether a decision was taken lawfully rather than whether it was the right one, so campaigners would need to show that the minister misread the law or left something important out.
Why Rosebank is a harder test

Rosebank, about 80 miles (130km) north west of Shetland, is the UK’s largest undeveloped oil field. Its operator’s own assessment puts the emissions from burning its oil and gas at up to 249 million tonnes over the life of the field, nearly seven times Jackdaw’s total. Fahnbulleh has already called it a different proposition, because its oil would be exported while Jackdaw’s gas flows straight into the UK system, and with only four refineries left in the country, much of it is expected to be refined in Europe.

This goes to the heart of the legal reasoning, because the Jackdaw decision leaned heavily on its gas being burned at home, within carbon budgets the government is bound to meet. That story is much harder to tell about oil sold on world markets, especially as the government’s guidance expects effects to be judged globally. A report by UCL researchers published last year argued that more UK oil means more global emissions, and any minister minded to approve Rosebank will need a persuasive answer.

The courts have not shut down the North Sea, then, but they have forced ministers to set out their climate reasoning in public before they say yes. Rosebank will reveal whether that reasoning still holds once the oil is shipped abroad.

articles.title: Jackdaw decision could haunt the UK at future climate summits
articles.author: Freddie Daley, Research Associate, Centre for Global Political Economy, University of Sussex
paras: Though the announcement that the UK government will move ahead with the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea was anticipated, it has generated a wave of criticism from around the world. This will have significant implications for the UK’s international standing on climate change.

The UK’s debate over new drilling has focused on job creation, energy security, emissions and the UK’s climate commitments, and the claim that the gas field was already licensed by the previous government.

Researchers and advocacy groups have poured cold water on these justifications, questioning the scale of the economic benefits of a project that will meet just 2% of UK gas demand for ten years – and that’s if none is exported.

The original consent for Jackdaw was quashed in 2025 for failing to account for its total emissions footprint – including those generated when the gas is actually burned. The field is owned by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian energy giant Equinor. The developers had to submit a fresh environmental assessment, and the government had to decide again whether to approve the project in light of the full emissions assessment. That means this is not an inherited decision: the government must own it outright.
Moving in the wrong direction

As more countries commit to phasing out fossil fuels and publish plans to do so, the UK government has moved in the opposite direction. By approving this project, the UK is showing that similar projects around the world are permissible, leaving its government with no grounds to object to fossil fuel projects elsewhere.

At the UN’s Cop30 climate summit in Brazil last year, the then energy secretary Ed Miliband said he was “fighting” for an outcome that contained a roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels. The UK joined over 80 countries in calling for the roadmap, acting in solidarity with countries already suffering the impacts of climate breakdown. Now the government is giving new drilling the go ahead. “That double standard”, said Mohamed Adow from the thinktank Power Shift Africa in response to the Jackdaw news, “will not go unnoticed”.

This blow to the UK’s credibility on climate was not inevitable. Despite the incredibly challenging backdrop of energy price shocks and supply bottlenecks, many governments are leaving fossil fuels in the ground. Our research shows that these policies range from bans and moratoriums on specific types of extraction or in certain areas, to fossil fuel subsidy reforms and restrictions on export credit. Many governments have begun working together on these policies as part of “climate clubs”, sharing best practice and pooling leverage.

Indeed the UK has pioneered many of these initiatives. It played a leading role in founding the Powering Past Coal Alliance and the Clean Energy Transition Partnership, which grew out of a UK policy. It was the first G7 nation to enshrine net zero into law and has made climate diplomacy a perennial feature of foreign policy across both Conservative and Labour governments.

What’s more, North Sea production is in long-term decline, with assets approaching retirement and employment declining for years. Meanwhile, renewable energy is making an increasing contribution to growth. If the UK can’t hold the line on new fossil fuel production and manage the phase-down of existing operations, what hope do less wealthy, less economically diversified countries have?
A global shift away from fossil fuels

A more fitting question is perhaps where true leadership is coming from. In 2027, governments will gather for the Second Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels – a process launched this year in Santa Marta, Colombia, and attended by countries representing one-third of global fossil fuel consumption and one-fifth of global production. Co-hosted by the governments of Ireland and Tuvalu, a low-lying island nation whose very existence is threatened by climate change, the conference offers a forum to develop coordinated measures to reduce dependence on fossil fuels, beyond the constraints of the annual UN climate summits where everyone gets a veto. In a world where multilateral cooperation is increasingly difficult, these governments are actively building a new geopolitics.

They are also facing down the reality of falling global demand for fossil fuels, with high-cost projects in declining basins like the North Sea most at risk when demand falls. The International Energy Agency expects peak demand for fossil fuels within four years. As sales of solar panels and electric vehicles accelerate at a dizzying pace in the wake of yet another global energy crisis, peak demand may come sooner than expected.

The legal ground has shifted too. The International Court of Justice produced an Advisory Opinion clarifying that failing to protect the climate through fossil fuel exploration and production may constitute an internationally wrongful act. Though the UK government’s own decision document rejects this, the Jackdaw decision is likely to trigger legal challenges.

The UK government now faces two challenges in quick succession. A decision on Rosebank, the UK’s largest untapped oil field, is still pending. And in early November, Andy Burnham and the UK delegation will arrive at the next UN climate summit, Cop31 in Antalya in Turkey.

Rejecting Rosebank may let the government draw a line under new production and recoup some semblance of leadership. But if Rosebank is approved, the UK will be providing a blueprint that any fossil fuel producer – established or prospective – can follow. Countries suffering from climate upheavals today, and upping the momentum to phase-out fossil fuels, will not let the UK forget it.

articles.title: Autumn wreaths and ‘doorscaping’: why we need more life in our front gardens
articles.author: James Simpson, Lecturer in Landscape Architecture, University of Sheffield
paras: There was a time when decorative wreaths appeared on front doors in December, stayed on front doors for a few weeks, and then disappeared.
Now red and gold autumn wreaths and Halloween wreaths are popping up everywhere. These seasonal displays are part of a wider social media fashion for “doorscaping”.

It is easy to see the appeal. A wreath introduces colour, foliage and a little seasonal personality without much effort. But this enthusiasm for decorating the front door raises an interesting possibility: could it encourage people to pay more attention to the garden immediately below?

Choosing a wreath and choosing plants for a front garden can both be ways of making the entrance to a home more attractive. A study of 1,000 people in England found that creating something beautiful was one motivation for front gardening. People motivated by appearance also tended to have greener front gardens.
That does not mean wreath enthusiasts will necessarily become gardeners. But the same interest in seasonal colour and decoration could encourage some to try planting around their front door.
And British front gardens could benefit from more planting.

The Royal Horticultural Society’s 2025 mapping estimates that 55% of front-garden space in Britain is paved, compared with 36% of back-garden space. Earlier RHS research found that the proportion of completely paved front gardens tripled between 2005 and 2015, although subsequent surveys suggested some recovery in planting.

Parking is one reason. An Ipsos survey found that, among people with largely paved front gardens or driveways, 28% said they needed the space for cars, while 45% thought it was too small for plants. Front gardens also have to accommodate access, bins and the everyday demands of domestic life.
But the cumulative effect of paving matters. One driveway can seem negligible. A street of them is a landscape.

This is where the appeal of seasonal decoration becomes useful. The seasonal colours and foliage that make a wreath attractive could also be found in plants growing around the front door. Someone who enjoys decorating their entrance might also be tempted to extend that interest into the garden.

A reused container, a few bulbs or a hardy perennial can be an inexpensive starting point. The RHS recommends containers for completely paved spaces, as well as climbers for walls and plants for otherwise unused corners.

Living plants do require some care. Pots need watering, and not everyone has the time, confidence or physical ability to maintain a garden. But starting with a few manageable plants offers a way to try growing something without committing to a complete redesign.

There may also be opportunities to go further. A strip beside a driveway or an unused corner could provide space for plants. Where practical, a few paving slabs could also be lifted to make room for planting. Parking and greenery do not have to be mutually exclusive.

These changes offer more than decoration. Flowers can provide nectar for insects, while shrubs and hedges offer shelter for wildlife. Larger plants, particularly trees and climbers, can provide shade and help keep buildings cooler in summer. Unlike impermeable paving, exposed soil and properly designed permeable surfaces can also help rainwater soak into the ground.

A study of more than 900 sites in front and back gardens and streets across England and Wales assessed combinations of grass, hedges, trees, shrubs and container plants. It found that mixtures of different plants generally performed better across several environmental measures, such as cooling or flood control, than just one type.
A pot of flowers cannot provide all these benefits, but it can still support insects and introduce planting where paving and parking have left little growing space.

Those decisions matter for new housing too. The 2026 Building for a Healthy Life design toolkit, a government guide to the design of housing developments, encourages space for planting in the front of houses.

But having space for plants is only part of the picture. People also need a reason to grow something. And this brings us back to the wreath. Its appeal lies in how easily people can add colour and character to the front of their homes.

If even some of that enthusiasm extended from the door to a pot, a border or a climbing plant, our streets could become more attractive and better for wildlife. If that interest grew to include more trees, shrubs and planted ground, it could also help our neighbourhoods cope better with heat and heavy rain.
What starts as a little seasonal decoration might become a lasting interest in growing plants.

articles.title: When climate data is transformed into visuals some people and places get overlooked
articles.author: Monika Frątczak, Postdoctoral Researcher, Digital Technologies, Communication and Artificial Intelligence, Manchester Metropolitan University
paras: When a climate disaster happens, people thousands of miles away may encounter it through numbers: how many people died, how many were displaced, how many homes were destroyed and how much infrastructure was damaged. But for the people living through it, the disaster is not a dataset. It is a home, a family, a livelihood and a place.
Billions of people around the world live in places and situations that are highly vulnerable to climate change, such as parts of Africa, Asia and small Pacific islands.

Data visualisations have become an important way of communicating climate change. Warming is represented through colours, emissions through lines and bars, and floods and fires through maps and animations. These visualisations can make an enormous and complicated problem easier to understand, but they can also shape how people feel about it.
Crucially, some visualisations don’t tell the full story.

I explored this in my new research with 34 social media users in the UK and Poland. I showed participants climate data visualisations and asked them how they felt and what they did with the information. Participants described worry, fear, sadness, anger and concern, but also curiosity, surprise and pleasure suggesting that visualisation can make unpalatable data more enjoyable.

The warming stripes for Poland (above) is a visualisation that shows temperature changes through coloured stripes. One participant said this visualisation looked “so pretty, nice and interesting”. But once they understood what the colours represented (red for warm temperatures; blue for cooler temperatures), their reaction changed, and the image became upsetting. The visualisation did more than show climate change: it changed how the participant experienced it.
What data visualisation leaves out

One of the most revealing moments in my research came from a meteorologist from Tonga who used to live in the UK. They first saw the warming stripes visualisation shared on social media, but Tonga was not shown as a location. They commented on the visualisation, asking whether stripes could be created for Tonga. They wanted to see what was happening at the scale of individual islands. They then went to the interactive version, where users can select locations to create their own stripes, but they could not create one for Tonga because the data wasn’t accessible for specific islands.

The visualisation showed temperature changes across broad regions, including the Pacific. But the participant wanted to see what was happening at the scale of particular islands. That visualisation prompted them to think about what could be done. They shared it with colleagues, and they decided to reproduce something similar using their own data.

The problem was not that the global visualisation was inaccurate. It was that accuracy at a global scale did not guarantee visibility at a local one. For communities such as those on Tonga (an island that contributes only a fraction of global emissions yet bears the brunt of climate change), this local visibility matters.

So who are visualisations making climate change “visible” for? For the participant from Tonga, climate change is closely connected to land, the sea, community and everyday life. They explained that data visualisation needs to reflect local context yet engage audiences more widely to convey an urgent need for climate action.
What happens after seeing the data

Climate data visualisation is not just a technical exercise. Researchers usually ask whether a graph is accurate, clear and easy to understand. But we should also ask who is represented, who is missing and whose experience the data allows us to see.

What people see can shape how they feel about climate change and what they believe they can do about it. My research found that emotional responses could lead people to share information, discuss it with others, change their everyday practices and sometimes inspire more formal political engagement.

But strong emotions did not automatically lead to action. People were more likely to describe taking direct climate action when they also felt there was something they could actually do at a local or national level. A sense of agency can help determine what happens after people encounter climate information.

The challenge for climate communication is not simply to find better and more accurate ways of showing the scale of the crisis. It is to ask whether, when climate change gets transformed into data, audiences are still able to see the people behind the numbers – and whether what is being shown gives people not only a reason to care, but a sense of what they can do.
Making climate change visible is only the first step. The harder and more critical challenge is considering whose experiences we see, whose are left out, and what happens after we see them.
Monika Frątczak receives funding from UKRI/ESRC.

articles.title: Chiricahua is the nation’s newest national park – what does that mean?
articles.author: Seth T. Kannarr, Visiting Honors Lecturer, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville
paras: With a stroke of a pen, President Donald Trump has officially created the United States’ 64th national park.

Chiricahua, in southeastern Arizona, was established as a national monument in April 1924 to protect its towering rhyolite hoodoos – tall spires of rock – and diversity of wildlife. The mountainous landscape is commonly known as a “wonderland of rocks.”

An act of Congress, signed by Trump, has now designated the 12,000-acre property a national park, the flagship label of the National Park Service system. It joins the Grand Canyon, Petrified Forest and Saguaro as the fourth national park in Arizona.

As a geographer who studies parks and the naming of places, I have seen that when a National Park Service property is redesignated as a national park, the new label doesn’t typically include much change for the site itself beyond signs and branding.

There’s not usually more money available to manage or protect the site. But the new title serves political purposes and could mean quite a lot to visitors, supporters and surrounding communities alike in the coming years.

The National Park Service manages 433 properties, which it calls units, with 19 different designations, such as “national battlefields,” “national lakeshores” and “national scenic trails.” Only 64 of these units carry the formal title or designation of “national park.”
All but one of these categories can be bestowed only by Congress. National monuments can be created by the president directly, under the provisions of the Antiquities Act of 1906.

For example, the Antiquities Act has been at the center of a decade-long controversy over the size of Bears Ears National Monument, which President Barack Obama created to protect 1.3 million acres in Utah in December 2016. Trump said that same act allowed him to shrink the protected area to 200,000 acres in 2017 and President Joe Biden to reexpand it to 1.3 million acres in 2021. In 2026, Trump slashed it again, to 121,000 acres, though lawsuits are contesting the action.
Why redesignations make a difference

My previous analysis of the contentious redesignation of the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial in St. Louis to Gateway Arch National Park in 2018 found that it was not done to offer additional protection for this monument to the United States’ Western exploration and growth.
Rather, the move was meant to take advantage of the public significance of the “national park” label and thereby attract more tourists and tourism revenue to the local economy.

The effort to make it a national park was part of a local campaign to renovate the underground visitor center, revitalize the park grounds and increase tourism. But the law that formalized the change included no additional funding, resources or protections for the Gateway Arch.

Changing the designation contradicted the park service’s own declaration that the term “national park” should be used for an area that “contains a variety of resources and encompasses large land or water areas to help provide adequate protection of the resources.”

During congressional hearings, the deputy director of the National Park Service, Robert Vogel, recommended the Gateway Arch not be labeled a national park but rather a national monument, because it “is too small and limited in the range of resources the site protects and interprets to be called a national park.”

Gateway Arch National Park is now the smallest-area park in the U.S., at less than 200 acres, and is home to a large steel arch, an open lawn area, a museum and a single historic building – a courthouse where one of the Dred Scott trials was heard, along with other civil rights cases.

However, it does not provide opportunities to view wildlife in its natural habitat, spectacular geologic features, diverse outdoor recreation opportunities or a sense of wilderness that the public has come to expect from national parks.
The park’s website admits “it is unusual for a national park to have no natural plant life” and describes the park as adjacent to the “concrete jungle of downtown St. Louis.”

Although Chiricahua’s rocky landscapes and archaeological evidence of long-standing Indigenous use and occupation more closely resembles what many people expect for a national park, it likely will receive some of the same public critique that the Gateway Arch and other national parks redesignated during the first Trump administration have received.
Potential ‘new’ national parks on the horizon
In rare cases, a community, group or other organization proposes adding an area that is not currently managed by the National Park Service to the system, but that process takes a lot of time.
It is more common to change the formal designation of a property already within the system, as has happened with this redesignation of Chiricahua.

Similarly, Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore became Indiana Dunes National Park in 2019. That same year, White Sands National Monument in New Mexico became White Sands National Park. And in 2020, New River Gorge National River in West Virginia became New River Gorge National Park and Preserve.

There are redesignation efforts underway seeking to make national parks in other locations as well, including the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, Apostle Islands National Lakeshore in Wisconsin, and Rock Creek Park in the District of Columbia.
In my measure, it is simply a waiting game to see whether these National Park Service sites will also be redesignated to national parks.
What will actually change for Chiricahua?

Making Chiricahua a national park was a bipartisan effort – co-sponsored by Arizona U.S. Reps. Juan Ciscomani, a Republican, and Greg Stanton, a Democrat – that has received some opposition for several reasons.

The complaints have highlighted fears that the new label will bring increased tourism and overcrowding in what is considered a small park with limited infrastructure. Now that Chiricahua has been redesignated, the potential influx of new visitors in the coming years could affect the more personal and isolated experience that they currently appreciate.

However, the only real changes in these places would be in marketing – the signs, brochures and merchandise sold in gift shops. But these changes have an important effect: The tagline of “new national park” markets well to potential visitors.

But the funding that Chiricahua receives from the federal government will not change, and the label of “national park” won’t actually protect this landscape any better than it already is under the stewardship of the National Park Service.
This article includes material previously published in an article about the potential redesignation of Ocmulgee Mounds on Dec. 8, 2025.
This article was updated on Oct. 27, 2026, to more clearly describe the legal controversy around the decreases in size to Bears Ears National Monument.

articles.title: El Niño is threatening California’s fragile coast again – the 1982-83 El Niño opened eyes to the serious erosion risks
articles.author: Gary Griggs, Distinguished Professor of Earth & Planetary Sciences, University of California, Santa Cruz
paras: California’s coastal bluffs and beaches look rugged, but they can be surprisingly fragile in the face of a powerful El Niño.

The state saw that in 1982-83, when storms amid one of the most destructive El Niño winters in California history battered the coastline with powerful waves and torrential rain, leaving hundreds of millions of dollars in damage in its wake. The storms coincided with elevated sea levels, high astronomical tides and very large waves delivered by repeated storms.

Extreme waves that winter destroyed one-third of the Santa Monica Pier and tore off large sections of the Huntington Beach Pier and the Paradise Cove Pier, while also damaging the Seal Beach, San Clemente and Malibu piers. Numerous seawalls, decks and stairways were torn apart, and 33 oceanfront homes were destroyed.
Massive waves also stripped millions of cubic yards of sand from Southern California beaches, and sections of the Pacific Coast Highway suffered severe flooding, mudslides and washouts.

Along the central coast, waves and high-tide flooding eroded bluffs. In Pacifica, just outside San Francisco, the edge of a sandy cliff lost over 65 feet as it failed, collapsing onto the beach and forcing the relocation of a two-story building and removal of an entire row of mobile homes. This area of high but weak bluffs continued to erode over the subsequent decades, forcing the demolition of bluff-top homes and apartments.

The El Niño now building in 2026-27 is forecast to be even stronger, and coastal homes are already seeing damage. I have studied coastal geology and oceanography in California for nearly six decades. With the conditions expected this year, coastal flooding, coastal erosion and landslides are likely, and more dramatic cliff collapses wouldn’t be a surprise, though every El Niño is different.
What is El Niño and why is it so destructive?

El Niño is one end of a climate pattern that swings from warm to cold every few years and can change weather patterns around the world. Normally dry areas can experience flooding rains, and wet areas can suffer droughts. The U.S. Pacific Coast in particular can take a beating from powerful atmospheric river storms with heavy downpours.

El Niños begin with a shift in wind patterns, which normally push warm waters from east to west along the equator. For reasons still not fully understood, the trade winds die and the warm pool of water in the western Pacific begins to flow back toward the coast of South America.
Part of this warm mass moves north toward the coast of California as a pulse or bulge, known as a Kelvin wave, and it begins to have far-ranging impacts.

Seawater expands as it warms, which raises sea level along the Pacific Coast for weeks during these periodic events. While all El Niños are not created equal, during the very large 1982-83 event, sea levels were elevated above predicted high tides by about a foot in San Diego to nearly 2 feet in San Francisco.
These higher sea levels can reach higher elevations and last longer.

The elevated sea levels also allow storm waves to break closer to the shoreline, eroding beaches and bluffs, leading to damage and destruction of both private oceanfront development and public infrastructure, including streets and highways, bridges and piers, and parks and recreational facilities.
Why California is vulnerable
Much of California’s coastal and shoreline development took place from the late 1940s to the late 1970s when the state’s population exploded.
Homes were built on beaches, bluffs and dunes during a period when the coastal storm climate was generally mild and there were no real concerns with coastal hazards and future sea-level rise.
This changed quickly in 1978 when the first strong El Niño in recent memory arrived, raising alarm about the hazards ocean development was exposed to.

The extreme 1982-83 El Niño that followed a few years later caused about US$328 million (in 2025 dollars) in damage to oceanfront property, $87 million in losses to recreational facilities such as piers, parking lots and access stairs, and $66 million in damage to large engineering structures such as breakwaters and jetties designed to protect harbors from storm waves.

At least in the short term, the 1982-83 El Niño winter changed popular perceptions of the stability or security of oceanfront homes and other shoreline development. Building restrictions were tightened, insurance rates rose, and many requests for new seawall permits were submitted.
But then it was back to business as usual, as new arrivals to the coast outbid each other for the same oceanfront homes damaged a few years before.

Increased coastal armoring, such as seawalls and rock revetments, helped limit erosion during other very large El Niños that followed, in 1997-98 and 2015-16, along with lucky timing that large waves arrived at low points in the monthly tidal cycle, leading to significantly less property damage than in 1982-83.

The coast was not so fortunate in winter 2022-23, when high seas and waves alone caused an estimated $4.7 billion in economic losses along California’s coast. The simultaneous occurrence of large storm waves, high tides and elevated sea levels were almost identical to the El Niño conditions in early 1983, 40 years earlier.
The state’s latest climate assessment, released Oct. 19, 2026, warns of more intense storms and increased erosion as temperatures increase and sea level continues to rise.
What will California see in 2026-27?

The southern end of the state is already suffering wave damage from an exceptionally busy Pacific hurricane season, also fueled by El Niño. Swells have stripped away beaches and destroyed homes in Southern California. The state’s storm season, when powerful atmospheric rivers bring downpours, typically begins in October or November and runs through early spring.
The magnitude of the emerging 2026-27 El Niño, likely to be one of the strongest on record, is making clear that coastal communities need to adapt now to a very different future.
How each coastal neighborhood, city and county responds will vary depending upon their local conditions and vulnerability to coastal erosion and flooding.

While many communities are stockpiling sandbags, clearing culverts and preparing evacuation plans, there are limits on what they can do to stop erosion. Building seawalls and rock revetments can provide some protection if well designed, but they can also create new problems, including leading to the loss of beaches over time as sea levels continue to rise. Putting more sand on beaches is costly and very short-lived.

Extensive shoreline development, eroding bluffs, aging infrastructure and increasing exposure to extreme weather are placing growing pressure on coastal communities and shorelines around the world. Some will eventually face the difficult transition from continued shoreline protection to retreating from the coast – either planned retreat or following repeated damage.

There is little that any developed coastal area can do at this point to minimize the impacts of the El Niño underway. What they can do is prepare to manage the risks and try to adapt to the changing future.

articles.title: Hot and cold climate extremes push UK’s energy system to its limits, new report reveals
articles.author: James Mollard, Researcher, School of Geosciences, University of Edinburgh
paras: The arrival of cooler weather following a summer of heatwaves, is a timely reminder that the UK electricity system must be resilient to the effects of temperature extremes at both ends of the thermometer.
The Royal Meteorological Society has released a new report that highlights how recent weather conditions have influenced electricity generation, demand and the infrastructure that connects them.

Authored by experts from the society, the Met Office and multiple UK universities, the State of the Climate for the UK Energy Sector Report 2025-26 shows that more energy is being provided by weather-dependent renewable sources. But high and low temperatures will continue to put the energy grid’s capacity and infrastructure to the test.

Data from the National Energy System Operator (Neso) shows that renewable energy formed a higher percentage of overall energy generated in the UK over the reporting period (April 2025 – March 2026) than any other year on record. The proportion coming from the combination of solar and wind increased, providing more than 38% of the nation’s electricity. The proportion of gas-powered generation reduced to 25%.

However, the report highlights how extreme weather tests the resilience of the grid. The conditions that lead to very high and low temperatures create different challenges through increasing electricity demand, limiting generation and damaging network infrastructure. The UK’s energy network is having to adapt to cope with increasingly extreme temperatures. In cold conditions, the network is put under strain due to increased heating demand. This requires more energy at short notice, increasing reliance on non-renewable sources.
For those responsible for balancing the electricity system, including Neso, these weather extremes can create operational challenges. This makes it harder to match energy supply with demand.

In early January 2026, strong northerly winds brought cold Arctic air, snow and ice into large parts of the UK. Initially these winds provided up to 20 gigawatts (GW) of power towards the system, a significant proportion of the demand.

But as the freeze reached its peak on the evening of January 6, the wind died down and wind generation fell to less than a quarter of the levels seen in the preceding days. Simultaneously, electricity demand peaked, with the increase in heating needs seeing demand peak an additional 5GW higher than the previous day.

Electricity supply and demand have to be kept in balance in real time. When demand rises or available generation falls, the energy system operator can maintain that balance by using additional generators to increase their output, for example. On this occasion, gas-powered electrical generation filled the gap by providing more than 25GW to the system at it’s peak.

This meant the demand was comfortably met, but this was an expensive strategy that meant the operator was paying up to £700 per megawatt-hour (MWh) for this generation. This was due to the higher cost of turning to gas generation, and the need for additional generation at short notice which costs more than generation that can be planned further in advance. This compares to the usual rate of just over £100 per MWh for the rest of January.
At the other end of the spectrum, hot temperatures are increasingly becoming more of a concern for the sector.

The summer of 2025 was the warmest on record at the time, with temperatures 1.51°C higher than average. During warmer temperatures, the network operator often limits the amount of power that transmission lines carry around the country to prevent components overheating. This reduces the risk of lines expanding more with heat which would make them sag and potentially short out on nearby vegetation or structures beneath.

Nevertheless, several faults in the network were attributed to heat causing infrastructure damage, leading to power cuts across parts of England, especially during two periods of heatwaves that occurred at the end of June and start of July.

In Europe, where temperatures also spiked, nuclear power plants were forced to limit output or shut down altogether because the water used to cool them with, taken from nearby rivers, was too warm. Increased temperatures and below-average rainfall also increased fire risks. The largest area lost to wildfire burning in the UK since satellite records began included a “mega-fire” in Scotland. Several of these fires led to localised power cuts across the country.
Preparing for future extremes

The UK’s new grid upgrade plan from the government, which aims to expand and modernise the British grid system to allow for connections to new generation sources and upgrades of current infrastructure, needs to consider the consequences of extreme temperatures. This includes ensuring that upgraded infrastructure can withstand the extreme heat we are now seeing more regularly in UK summers, as well as ensuring that capacity for transmission of electricity from generation sources to population centres is increased.

Delays to electricity grid upgrades risk higher consumer bills as the operator is required to pay wind farms to stop generating because electricity produced cannot be be carried to where it is needed, replacing it with more local gas-powered generation instead.

The resilience of the UK grid has stood up well to the challenges it faced from the weather in the past year. But maintaining that resilience requires continued investment and adaptation as the climate, energy needs of the nation and profile of energy generation all continue to change.

articles.title: Wild fish are a precious resource – here’s how aquaculture can bolster food security
articles.author: Wesley Malcorps, Research Fellow, Institute of Aquaculture, University of Stirling
paras: Small fish such as sardinella are an affordable source of protein and essential nutrients for millions of people across West Africa.

Some of these fish are increasingly exported or processed into fishmeal and fish oil for aquaculture feeds used in high-income European countries and across East Asia, particularly China. As nutrient deficiencies are common in people living in parts of West Africa, retaining more fish for local consumption could help improve diets and address dietary health problems.

Aquaculture is one of the world’s fastest-growing food production sectors. Despite its growth in the last three decades, global wild fish catches for marine ingredients have declined overall. Production has increased in some regions, including West Africa, but the overall decline is mainly due to improved fishery management that allows recovery of fish stocks.

Globally, a quarter of wild-caught fish are processed into fishmeal and fish oil, and only a small share originates from West Africa. Most is used in animal feed, with aquaculture accounting for the largest share. These provide valuable nutrients, particularly in early-life-stage diets and for carnivorous species such as salmon and shrimp, while contributing to the relatively low carbon footprint of farmed seafood.

The supply of marine ingredients is highly regulated and fairly stable but should not be taken for granted. Climate change and warming periods such as El Niño can weaken the upwelling of nutrient-rich waters from the deep sea. This reduces the availability of plankton and fish and limits the supply of marine ingredients required for aquaculture.

This means we need to make the best use of the resources already available. Fish processing by-products (including heads, guts and skeletons) are playing an increasingly important role, accounting for 34% of global fishmeal production and 54% of fish oil supply in 2024.
A new era of supply chain risk

Marine ingredients from potentially unsustainable sources have slipped through the net despite responsible sourcing claims. One 2025 investigation found that certified Turkish-farmed seabass sold by major retailers in Europe was fed fishmeal sourced from three factories in Senegal that have been linked to food insecurity and job losses in local communities.

One way to reduce risk in aquaculture feed supply chains is to source ingredients domestically. But this is easier said than done. Aquafeed supply chains are dependent on the global trade in marine and terrestrial ingredients and thus face challenges related to scale, cost, nutritional quality and environmental sustainability.

While marine ingredients can be sustainably sourced and continue to be essential to the global food system, it’s important to use them in efficient ways that maximise their contribution to human nutrition. Certification programmes currently focus on ensuring that fish are caught or farmed responsibly. The environmental and social safeguards include stock status, environmental footprint and making sure workers are treated fairly.

The certification programmes pay less attention to food security and critics argue they favour export markets and corporations over local communities. As a result, calls are growing for broader measures of what constitutes truly sustainable and ethical seafood.

Some scientists argue that fish, such as anchovies and mackerel, provide more essential nutrients when eaten directly rather than used as feed. Most species used in the marine ingredients industry have low market appeal and limited consumer demand, meaning that diverting fish from feed to food does not automatically improve food security.

Peru’s anchoveta fishery is the world’s largest fish stock used to produce marine ingredients. Despite its scale and nutritional value, there has been low demand for anchoveta as a food fish within Peru. Factors such as low demand, short shelf life, limited logistics and strong economic incentives to process fish into fishmeal and fish oil have often hindered the development of markets for some fish as food. Strategic use of some fish as feed can help convert marine resources into nutritious and accessible seafood.

To make the most of limited marine resources, the aquaculture industry could improve how it tracks fish and nutrients as they are transformed into farmed seafood. We have developed a novel peer-reviewed performance tool that provides a common sustainability language. At the heart of the tool is the Fish In: Fish Out (Fifo) ratio, a measure of how efficiently fish, and the omega-3 fatty acids they contain, are converted into farmed fish.

Efficiency can be improved by increasing the use of fish processing by-products that are not normally eaten by people and by strategically replacing certain marine ingredients with alternatives such as algal oil and insect meal. The tool is currently being used by a variety of organisations like feed and ingredient companies, farmers, environmental charities, and researchers.

Applying the tool in our latest study already challenged conventional thinking about marine ingredient use in aquaculture. Although Faroese salmon is often viewed as a major consumer of marine ingredients, we found it was actually a net producer of edible omega-3 fatty acids. This was achieved by upcycling valuable nutrients from inedible sources (fishery by-products) into a nutritious farmed product, without increasing the need for fish that could be consumed directly by humans.

Making the most of limited marine resources is important, but decisions made in one country can affect food availability and affordability elsewhere. Therefore, harmonising nutrition-sensitive policies across local, national and regional levels is crucial to achieve meaningful outcomes. Traceability systems can play an important role, but they must do more than track supply chains.

They can only make a meaningful difference when they empower local communities through greater participation in decision-making and improved market access. They should support those closest to the resource, rather than treating them simply as sources of data for downstream companies. In West Africa, this could include retaining a proportion of the catch for local consumption and improving the cold chain to support its distribution.

These approaches would enable the marine ingredients and aquaculture industries to operate effectively. They would also contribute more to global food security, the economy and the supply of nutritious seafood to consumers.
